entry.title: Stop Managing SAP BTP Role Collections by Hand — Let Terraform Do It
entry.content:
GIT repository link :  LinktoGithub 

Problem

We had around 150 users across SAP BTP subaccounts, each needing different role collections. For a while we handled it manually — logging into the cockpit, clicking through assignments, hoping nothing was missed.

The issues were predictable:

  • No audit trail of who assigned what and when
  • Onboarding a new user meant someone had to remember to do it
  • Removing access when someone left was a manual checklist item that occasionally got skipped
  • Nobody had a clear picture of the current state unless they clicked through every user

We needed something repeatable, reviewable, and not dependent on someone remembering to do it.

Approach

The SAP BTP Terraform provider (SAP/btp) has a resource called btp_subaccount_role_collection_assignment that handles exactly this. The idea was simple:

  • Keep a CSV file as the single source of truth for who has what roles
  • Let Terraform compare that CSV against the actual BTP state
  • Apply only the diff — add what's missing, remove what's no longer needed

The CSV looks like this:

email,roles
ajay@company.com,Subaccount Viewer 
shalini@company.com,Extension Center - Administrator;Subaccount View

Multiple roles per user are semicolon-separated on one row. Terraform explodes each row into individual email::role resource pairs and manages them independently.

Handling existing users safely

The tricky part was not starting from scratch. We already had assignments in BTP made manually through the cockpit. If Terraform doesn't know about them, it won't touch them — but anything it creates and then doesn't see in the CSV, it will destroy.

The safe onboarding sequence was:

  1. Export all current assignments from BTP into the CSV format using a Python script against the BTP Security API
  2. Generate terraform import commands for every existing assignment
  3. Run the imports — this loads current BTP state into Terraform's state file
  4. Run terraform plan — should show zero changes if the export was complete
  5. From that point, Terraform owns all assignments

Once the state file and CSV matched BTP reality, we had full confidence that any future apply would only touch what we intended.

Day-to-day usage

After the one-time setup, the workflow is:

Edit role_assignments.csv  →  terraform plan  →  terraform apply
  • For New user needs roles --> Add a row to the CSV, apply.
  • For User needs an extra role --> Append it to their row, apply.
  • For User leaving --> Delete their row, apply. Terraform revokes all their assignments.
  • For User in BTP but no roles yet --> Don't add a CSV row until they need one — the live BTP data source skips users who haven't activated their account, so no apply failures.

The terraform plan step is the safety net. It shows exactly what will change before anything touches BTP — green for additions, red for removals. If the plan looks wrong, fix the CSV and plan again. Nothing changes until you explicitly apply.

What we used

  • Terraform with the SAP BTP provider (~> 1.9)
  • btp_subaccount_role_collection_assignment resource
  • btp_subaccount_users data source (live user validation before each apply)
  • Python script for the one-time BTP export
  • csvdecode() + flatten() + for_each in Terraform locals for the multi-role explosion logic

All 10 files are there. Here's a summary of what each does:

File Purpose When to touch

export_roles.pyExports BTP → CSVOnce, before first apply
generate_imports.pyGenerates import.shOnce, after export
main.tfCore Terraform logicNever (unless logic changes)
providers.tfSAP BTP provider configNever
variables.tfVariable definitionsNever
outputs.tfShows results after applyNever
role_assignments.csvUser → role mappingEvery time roles change
terraform.tfvarsYour account IDsFill in once
terraform.tfvars.exampleSafe template to commitNever
.gitignoreProtects secrets/stateNever

The only file you edit day-to-day is role_assignments.csv.

What this solved

Every role change is now a file edit + two commands. The CSV in version control is the audit trail — you can see who changed what and when through git history. Onboarding is consistent. Offboarding is reliable. And nobody needs cockpit access just to assign a role collection.

If you're managing more than a handful of users in BTP, this setup is worth the one-time investment.

What's next

One thing worth exploring is wrapping this in a GitHub PR workflow. The idea is simple — role_assignments.csv lives in a Git repository, and any change to it goes through a pull request. A reviewer approves the role change, merge triggers terraform apply automatically. You get a full audit trail in Git history without any extra tooling, and no one can bypass the process by editing the file directly on main. Something to consider as the team grows.

entry.title: Public Release of the MCP server for SAP BTP administration
entry.content:
If you manage infrastructure on SAP BTP, you know the friction of context switching. Getting a simple answer about your landscape usually means either clicking through deep hierarchies in the SAP BTP Cockpit or stringing together a chain of BTP CLI commands where the output of one feeds into the input of the next.

Today, we are announcing the public availability of the MCP server for SAP BTP administration. Delivered as a remote endpoint, it bridges the gap between Large Language Models and your BTP environment, allowing you to query, manage, and provision resources using natural language via any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Talk to Your Infrastructure

The goal isn't to replace the Cockpit or the CLI, but to remove the cognitive load of navigating them for declarative tasks. By pointing an MCP-compatible client (like Claude desktop or Claude Code) to our endpoint, you can just ask questions about your system:

  • Discovery: "What entitlements are currently available in my subaccounts from the US-East region?"
  • Auditing: "Is user foo@bar.com onboarded and assigned the correct roles for this project across all our production subaccounts?"
  • Provisioning: "Create a new subaccount for the QA team that mirrors the exact entitlements and user access of the Staging subaccount."

Instead of writing custom scripts to fetch IDs, parse JSON, and execute subsequent commands, your agent uses the remote MCP server to dynamically sequence the right API calls based on your intent.

Zero Footprint, Zero Privilege Escalation

When exposing infrastructure APIs to AI agents, security and setup friction are the primary concerns. We designed this as a remote service to be completely frictionless for the user.

  • Zero Platform Setup: There is no source code to compile, no infrastructure to host, no destinations to configure and no proxy apps to deploy on your BTP subaccounts. You simply add the remote endpoint and Client ID to your local MCP configuration, and it works.
  • Principal Propagation via SAP IDS: Authentication is handled via the Authentication Code Flow through SAP's Default Identity Provider. This means the AI agent operates strictly under your user principal. The tool never has more access than you do, ensuring all existing IAM policies and role collections are strictly enforced.
  • Cross-Region by Default: Just like using the Cockpit or the CLI, you only need to connect once. The server handles the regional routing behind the scenes, giving you immediate access to all your BTP resources across all regions without needing to juggle endpoints.

Get Started in Minutes

The MCP server for SAP BTP administration is live today as a remote service. To connect your MCP application, you only need our endpoint URL and a public Client ID enabled for SAP IDS:

claude mcp add --transport http btp-administration \
  "https://sso.mcp.btp.cloud.sap/mcp" \
  --client-id e789ba01-5612-47ee-bfe7-79e26411c1ca

Note: Be sure to check the official documentation for the exact connection parameters and supported clients.

entry.title: Who Still Has Access to My SAP BTP Subaccount?
entry.content:
Reconciling SAP BTP Shadow Users with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using n8n 

Removing Identity and access is one of the most important parts of the identity lifecycle. 

When a user becomes inactive in SAP Cloud Identity Services, the expectation is usually that the user should no longer retain unnecessary access in connected systems. But how do we verify that the expected deprovisioning has actually happened in an SAP BTP subaccount?

That question led me to build this n8n workflow:

Can I retrieve users from SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP BTP, compare them using their email addresses, and identify BTP users whose IAS identity is inactive or missing?

The workflow retrieves users from both systems through OAuth-protected APIs, normalizes the API responses, compares the users by email address, and generates a CSV report containing the invalid users.   

I also added an optional branch that can delete an invalid BTP user. That branch is intentionally deactivated by default and should only be used after appropriate validation and approval if needed.

This blog will talk about how to build an n8n workflow that could automate user reconciliation.

Why I Built This

Provisioning solutions are normally designed to move identities from a source system to target applications.

But successful provisioning does not automatically answer this question:

Does the target system still contain users who should no longer be there?

For one user, this can be checked manually:

Search for the user in SAP Cloud Identity Services. Check whether the identity is active. Search for the same user in the SAP BTP subaccount. Compare the two records. Record the result.

This approach is manageable for one or two users, but it becomes repetitive and error prone as the user population grows.

I did not want to download two files and maintain a collection of spreadsheet formulas. I wanted a repeatable workflow that could retrieve the current records, apply the same matching logic every time, and produce a file that could be reviewed. 

Provisioning tells us what should have happened. Reconciliation helps us verify what actually exists in the target platform.

Scope note: this pattern only sees identities that actually traverse IAS. If a population is provisioned into BTP through some other path / IGA tools, this workflow won't catch drift there - confirm your own provisioning paths before treating this as a complete control.

What We Are Building

The workflow is intentionally simple. SAP Cloud Identity Services and BTP users are retrieved and normalized separately, after which BTP users are compared against IAS using the normalized email address. The n8n workflow contains the following nodes: 

Schedule Trigger
  ↓
Get IAS Users
  ↓
Normalize IAS Users
  ↓
Get BTP Users
  ↓
Normalize BTP Users
  ↓
Compare and Find Invalid Users
  ↓
Filter Invalid Users
  ↓ (Kept)
  ├── Convert to File (CSV export — audit evidence)
  └── Delete Invalid BTP User (Deactivated) — disabled by default

An optional BTP deletion branch is connected after the invalid-user filter, but it remains disabled by default. The reporting flow can therefore be tested independently without deleting the user.

Prerequisites

Before starting, you need:

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Tenant
  • IAS Technical system with user read permission 
  • SAP BTP Cloud Foundry Subaccount 
  • An XSUAA Service instance and service Key
  • n8n self-hosted or on a trial (community edition is free to self-host indefinitely for internal use) 

I am using SAP BTP Trial platform and n8n trial (community edition) for this scenario.

Authentication Design

Both API integrations use OAuth-based authentication in this workflow. Of course, you can use Basic authentication for IAS API call.

 IAS Authentication

I have created technical system in IAS Administration console and assigned required access. The technical system provides the client credentials needed by n8n to request an access token.

The IAS user endpoint follows this pattern:

GET https://<ias-tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/scim/Users

The Identity Directory API exposes SCIM resources for users, groups, and custom schemas.

BTP Authentication

For SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I used an XSUAA service key.

The XSUAA REST APIs support programmatic administration of security artifacts, including users, roles, and role collections. An XSUAA instance using the appropriate API access plan provides the URL and credentials required for the REST calls.

 

The service key provides values such as:

Client ID
Client Secret
OAuth URL
API URL

In my US10 trial environment, the BTP user endpoint is:

GET https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users

The endpoint is region-specific, so should use the API URL provided by own XSUAA service configuration.

Part 1 – Build It

Step 1: Define the Reconciliation Rules

Before creating the comparison logic, I defined the possible outcomes.

Valid user

A BTP user is classified as VALID when:

The BTP user has an email AND exactly one IAS user has the same normalized email AND The IAS user is active

The resulting reason code is: IAS_USER_ACTIVE

Invalid user

A BTP user is classified as INVALID in either of these cases: No IAS user has the same email

Result: IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

Or:

One IAS user has the same email AND The IAS user is inactive

Result: IAS_USER_INACTIVE

This distinction matters because a data-quality problem should not automatically become a deletion decision.

Step 2: Retrieve IAS Users

The first HTTP Request node is named: Get IAS Users

The node calls the IAS Identity Directory SCIM endpoint:  

GET https://<ias-tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/scim/Users

The access token is obtained through the OAuth credential configured in n8n. A simplified IAS user from my test looked like this:

The IAS SCIM interface supports user retrieval and filtering through attributes such as emails.value. It also supports pagination using parameters such as startIndex and count.

Step 3: Normalize IAS Users

The IAS response is passed to: Normalize IAS Users

This is an n8n Code node using JavaScript. The normalization step reduces every IAS user to the fields required for reconciliation:

The normalization logic:

  • Reads the SCIM Resources array
  • Selects the primary email when available
  • Falls back to the first populated email
  • Removes leading and trailing spaces
  • Converts the email address to lowercase
  • Preserves the IAS user ID
  • Preserves the IAS active status as a Boolean

Step 4: Retrieve BTP Users

The next HTTP Request node is: Get BTP Users

For my Cloud Foundry trial environment, it calls: 

GET https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users

A simplified BTP user from the trial looked like this:

Step 5: Normalize BTP Users

The BTP response is passed to: Normalize BTP Users 

This Code node creates a consistent representation of each BTP user:

The email-selection logic follows this order:

  1. Use the primary email when available.
  2. Otherwise, use the first populated value in emails[].
  3. If the email array is empty, use userName when it contains an email address.
  4. If needed, use externalId when it contains an email address.

Step 6: Why I Compared Email Instead of Username 

It depends on Application subject Name identifier - BTP username could be such as Global UserID, Email, LoginName, UserID etc. But email will be same in both IAS and BTP.

The IAS record contained:

IAS userName: test.user04

The BTP record contained:

BTP userName: testuser04@invalid.example

A direct username comparison would classify these as different users.

The email values, however, were the same:

IAS emails[].value: testuser04@invalid.example

BTP emails[].value: testuser04@invalid.example

For this reason, the workflow compares users using a normalized version of:  emails[].value and The normalization applies: 

String(email ?? '') .trim() .toLowerCase();

This means the following values are treated as equal:

TestUser04@Invalid.Example
testuser04@invalid.example

Step 7: Compare and Find Invalid Users

The node first creates an index of the normalized IAS users: 

Normalized email
↓
IAS user record

Each BTP user is then checked against that index.

For the test user, the workflow found:

BTP user exists: Yes
BTP active: true
IAS email match: Yes
IAS active: false
IAS match count: 1

The result was:

The BTP account is active, but the corresponding IAS identity is inactive. The workflow therefore sends the record to the invalid-user branch. Specific reason codes make the CSV report easier to understand and troubleshoot.

Step 8: Filter Invalid Users

The comparison results are passed to: Filter Invalid Users. The filter keeps records where: validationStatus = INVALID

This includes:

IAS_USER_INACTIVE

IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

Users classified as VALID are removed from the exception path.

Step 9: Generate the CSV Report

I used "convert to File" node to store the generated invalid user's list so that I can review and delete later after validation.

The output destination can be changed to OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, SFTP, or another controlled repository.

Step 10: Optional Deletion of Invalid BTP Users

A second branch is connected after: Filter Invalid Users.  The branch contains: Delete Invalid BTP User

The node is deactivated by default. When This node is activated, the node can issue a request conceptually similar to:

DELETE https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users/<BTP_USER_ID>

The operation uses the BTP user ID returned by the API.

The user ID is safer for targeting the technical record than using the email address alone.

Testing Final Workflow 

Let's see IAS User's list. As I am using trial account, so it is easy count users and remember user's status. 

Here is BTP Users list who has been login. You might notice the difference in BTP user because I did not login in BTP applications using that id.

I will run the n8n workflow without enabling Delete invalid BTP user node. 

Workflow run successfully and provided all invalid user's list in CSV file

Let's check how CSV looks like. 

In CSV, you can check why users are marked as invalid as either user is not active in IAS or does not exist in IAS anymore. 

To delete user

I will enable Delete Invalid BTP User node

Once I will execute this workflow, user should be deleted from BTP subaccount. 

Workflow run successfully.

And users are deleted in subaccounts as well.

As we save invalid records in CSV, you can review how many users are invalid and deleted.

Troubleshooting 

 

Problem

Likely Cause

 What to Check

IAS normalization returns no users

The API response is stored as a JSON string under data.

inspect typeof item.json.data 

The diagnostic output shows thousands of data keys

Object.keys() was called on a string instead of a parsed object.

JavaScript returns character positions: 0 1 2 3

IAS and BTP users do not match

The comparison is using userName.

Compare IAS emails[].value with BTP emails[].value

The BTP email has primary: false

The normalization accepts only an email where primary is true.

Use the primary email when one exists. Otherwise, use the first populated value in the email array.

Every BTP user appears to be missing from IAS

The IAS response was not parsed

IAS totalResults

The deletion node does not execute

The node is deactivated.

active the node for execution

 

Part 2 – Production Hardening

Prefer certificate-based auth over client secrets where it's supported

Client credentials with a shared secret work fine for a POC, but a long-lived secret sitting in a credential store is still a static value someone could leak or need to rotate. Where the target API supports mTLS/X.509-bound OAuth clients, that's the stronger option for a production reconciliation job.

Use least-privileged credentials

The reconciliation path should use read-only permissions wherever possible.

The deletion operation should use a separate, tightly controlled credential rather than sharing the same credential used for reporting.

Keep credentials in the n8n credential store. Do not place client IDs, client secrets, access tokens, or authorization headers in:

  • Code nodes
  • Workflow notes
  • Screenshots
  • CSV files
  • Exported templates
  • Source-control repositories

Recheck IAS before deletion

The user’s status may change between the original comparison and the deletion action.

Before deletion, call IAS again using an email filter: emails.value eq "<candidate-email>"

The deletion should stop if: 

The IAS user is now active
Multiple IAS users match
The IAS API call fails
The IAS response cannot be parsed
The BTP user ID no longer matches
The email has changed

Protect special accounts

Some identities should not pass through a generic deletion rule:

  • Emergency accounts
  • Break-glass administrators
  • Technical users
  • Integration users
  • Service accounts
  • Tenant administrators
  • Privileged support users
  • Accounts used for business continuity

These identities should be excluded or routed to a separate review process.

Implement Pagination

This is the most important known limitation. 

The IAS SCIM API supports pagination through values such as: startIndex, count, totalResults, itemsPerPage

The same completeness check must be applied to the BTP endpoint.

The intended process is:

Request the first page
↓
Read totalResults
↓
Calculate the next startIndex
↓
Request the next page
↓
Combine the results
↓
Stop when all users have been retrieved

Without pagination, a valid IAS identity located on a later page may not be present in the n8n comparison data.

The workflow could then incorrectly classify the corresponding BTP user as:

IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

For that reason:

The deletion branch should not be activated for a production population until complete pagination has been implemented and tested for both IAS and BTP.

Monitor the reconciliation workflow

A failed reconciliation can create a misleading result.

If the workflow stops running, no exception report is generated. That silence could be mistaken for a clean environment.

A production implementation should include:

  • An n8n Error Trigger workflow
  • Failure notification
  • Last-success monitoring
  • Retrieved-user count monitoring
  • Alerts for unusual count changes
  • Execution logs
  • A heartbeat or watchdog process

Preserve an audit trail

For each execution, retain: 

Execution timestamp
IAS tenant or environment
BTP subaccount
IAS totalResults
Normalized IAS user count
BTP totalResults
Normalized BTP user count
Valid user count
Invalid user count
Review user count
CSV filename
Deletion enabled or disabled
Deletion result
Error details

The report contains identity information, so it must be protected according to the organization’s security, privacy, and retention requirements.

 

Final Thought 

I started with one question:

Does every user in my SAP BTP subaccount still have an active identity in SAP Cloud Identity Services?

The workflow can now answer that question for my trial environment.

The same pattern could be extended to:

  • Reconcile users across multiple BTP subaccounts
  • Identify privileged users with inactive identities
  • Detect unexpected identity-provider origins
  • Create ServiceNow review tasks
  • Notify a Microsoft Teams security channel
  • Maintain reconciliation evidence in an IAM governance platform
  • Track unresolved deprovisioning exceptions
  • Detect technical users mixed with employee identities

Not every IAM control requires a large implementation.

A small, clearly bounded workflow can still make identity differences visible and provide useful evidence. The key is knowing where automated reporting ends and where controlled remediation begins.

What other SAP BTP identity reconciliation scenarios would you automate?

Disclaimer

This workflow was created and tested in an SAP trial environment using one controlled test identity. 

It is not an SAP-delivered BTP user-reconciliation capability. n8n is an external workflow orchestration platform.

The current workflow does not implement complete pagination for IAS or BTP. The workflow should therefore not be used for production deletion until pagination, approval, revalidation, exclusion rules, exception handling, monitoring, and recovery procedures have been implemented and tested.

The Delete Invalid BTP User node is deactivated by default and must be deliberately enabled.

Before adopting a similar pattern in production, review the organization’s requirements for:

  • Identity governance
  • Joiner, mover, and leaver processing
  • Change approval
  • Privileged-access protection
  • API credential management
  • Personal-data handling
  • Audit logging
  • Data retention
  • Incident management
  • Recovery and rollback

Do not delete a BTP user solely because the user appears in a generated CSV. Revalidate the identity and use an approved IAM lifecycle or administrative process.

References

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Directory API
    Identity Directory SCIM API and technical-system authorization prerequisites. Identity Directory API | SAP Help Portal
  • SAP BTP, Administration APIs of the Authorization and Trust Management Service
    Overview of APIs for users, roles, role collections, identity providers, and security settings. Accessing Administration Using APIs of the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service | SAP Help Portal
  • n8n, Convert to File
    Converting workflow data into CSV and other file formats. Convert to File | Nodes | n8n Docs

entry.title: Orchestrating SAP BTP Administration with n8n and the MCP Server
entry.content:
We recently introduced the MCP server for SAP BTP administration to let you manage your infrastructure using natural language from your favorite AI clients. But what if you want to take those conversational capabilities and weave them into automated, repeatable processes?

Today, we present an additional integration outside from the already mentioned harnesses in the SAP Help documentation: n8n.

What is n8n?

n8n is a powerful low-code workflow automation tool that provides a visual canvas for orchestrating AI, code, and APIs across your entire tech stack. It allows you to build complex sequences that connect disparate systems, process data, and trigger actions driven by specific business logic. By bridging the gap between traditional, deterministic automation and the dynamic reasoning of modern AI, n8n helps teams safely integrate AI agents into their daily operations.

Currently, you can build these workflows right away if you are running a self-managed n8n instance. However, looking ahead, this setup will become completely seamless. Through a strategic partnership, n8n will soon be available as a fully managed environment on the SAP Business AI Platform. This means SAP software developers will be able to visually build AI workflows and orchestrate agents natively, drawing from existing BTP credits without the need to set up extra infrastructure.

Nonetheless, even if that fully managed environment isn't still rolled out, you can still connect our new remote MCP endpoint to your self-managed n8n instance and drag and drop your way to intelligent SAP BTP workflows right now!

Integration with MCP Server for SAP BTP Administration

You can arm a no-code AI agent with the tools to independently troubleshoot typical account or connectivity issues, or you can insert specific platform management tools as guaranteed steps in a larger deterministic sequence, and everything happens visually through the MCP Client Node:

How you wire this node dictates how it behaves. If you place it as a standalone step in a traditional flow, you will select a single, specific administrative tool for n8n to execute at that exact moment. If you wire it into an AI Agent, you instead select a broad range of tools to expose. The agent then dynamically decides which tools to call depending on the overarching task you give it.

Once your node is placed, it is time to establish the connection. You will paste in the endpoint URL for the remote MCP Server:

https://sso.mcp.btp.cloud.sap/mcp

For authentication, select MCP OAuth2 from the dropdown and click the button "Set up credential" to set up a new authentication process. Setting up this credential requires a little precision because we are authenticating securely against SAP IDS using a public PKCE client.

First, you must uncheck the Use Dynamic Client Registration box. The SAP authorization server requires you to supply the Client ID explicitly rather than registering dynamically:

With dynamic registration off, set your Grant Type to PKCE. You can then fill in the standard routing details:

Grant TypeAuthorization Code
Authorization URLhttps://accounts.sap.com/oauth2/authorize
Access Token URLhttps://accounts.sap.com/oauth2/token
Client IDe789ba01-5612-47ee-bfe7-79e26411c1ca
Scopeopenid

There is one final, crucial trick to making this connection work. Because this is a public PKCE client, there is no client secret. The n8n interface, however, strictly requires a value in the Client Secret field to let you save the form. To satisfy the UI without breaking the authentication flow, hover over the Client Secret field and switch it into Expression mode. Leave the expression completely blank. The interface will display a helpful [empty] tag, letting you know it registered the blank state correctly.

Save your new credentials, and the MCP server is fully integrated!

Note: Remember that AI-tools are evolving at a rapid rate! Be sure to check the official n8n documentation just in case some configuration steps for the MCP Client Node change in the future.

entry.title: SAP GRC Access Control Risk Analysis to SAP BTP (XSUAA)
entry.content:
1. Introduction

SAP GRC Access Control is commonly used as the central governance layer for access requests, approvals, risk analysis, provisioning, and audit trails. However, SAP BTP role collections are not covered by a standard GRC connector, even though BTP is increasingly part of hybrid landscapes alongside S/4HANA and other enterprise applications.

The provisioning side of this integration is described in my previous SAP Community blog Access Provisioning in SAP BTP Using SAP GRC Access Control 12.0. It shows how to use a custom IF_GRAC_AD_ACCESS_MGMT  adapter with the standard MSMP workflow and provisioning framework to assign and remove BTP role collections through XSUAA and SCIM APIs.

This blog builds on that foundation and addresses the other part of the governance problem: Risk Analysis. It explains how a custom IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT adapter reads the BTP authorization model - user → role collection → role → scope, and maps it into the structures that the standard GRC AC risk-analysis engine already understands. 

The result is a single governance flow in which GRC can request and provision BTP access, analyze that access against SoD rules, and retain the approval, provisioning, risk, and audit context in the same platform.

There is no delivered adapter for SAP BTP subaccounts where authorizations are managed by XSUAA (role collections → roles → scopes). So we built:

  • ZCL_BTP_XSUAA_CLIENT : An internal REST client that talks to XSUAA (SCIM users & groups and the authorization v2 API for role collection detail and role scopes).
  • ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP : The IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT  implementation GRC AC calls during risk analysis.
  • ZCL_GRAC_AD_ACCESS_MGMT_BTP :  Implements the provisioning integration and is outside this blog’s scope.

Connector configured in GRC AC:

  • Connector: ZBTP_XSUAA_API_*******
  • Connector type: HTTP RFC destinations for the token endpoint and the API endpoint.

For the initial configuration and setup, including BTP credentials, SM59 destinations, connector creation, SPRO configuration, and provisioning-adapter registration, refer to the provisioning blog. This article assumes that foundation is already in place and focuses on authorization retrieval and SoD risk analysis.

 

2. The BTP Authorization Model

 

BTP ObjectAnalogous ABAP Object
User(SCIM) with originABAP SU01 user
Role collection (SCIM Group)Composite role
Role (instance of a role template inside an XSUAA app)Single role
Scope - string of the form xsappname.object.path.verbAuthorization object and activity

A user is a member of one or more role collections. A role collection contains role references. Each role has a list of scopes. That chain - user → role collection → role → scope - is what the risk-analysis engine needs to understand technically. ZCL_BTP_XSUAA_CLIENT implements this traversal by resolving the user's role collections, their associated roles, and the scopes granted by each role.

Authorization flow

Application
     -> Role Template
            -> Scope
     -> Role
            -> Role Collection
                   -> User

When the following command is executed with the BTP CLI, the JSON response shows the role-template metadata, scopes, and scope descriptions:

btp --format json get security/role "aicore_batch_admin" \
  --of-app "aicore!b164" \
  --of-role-template "aicore_batch_admin"

 

{
  "roleTemplateName": "aicore_batch_admin",
  "roleTemplateAppId": "aicore!b164",
  "name": "aicore_batch_admin",
  "description": "Edit batches in AI Core",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "name": "aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write",
      "description": "create, update and delete batches"
    },
    {
      "name": "aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.read",
      "description": "get batches"
    }
  ]
}

The scope "name": "aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write" consists of the following components:

Component

Value

Meaning

xsappname

aicore!b164

Application identifier

object

scenarios

Main business object or domain

path

batches

Sub-resource or functional path

verb

write

Permitted operation

 

3. Extracting BTP Authorizations for SoD Risk Analysis

The provisioning article describes the general XSUAA integration and SCIM provisioning calls. This section focuses only on the read path required by the GRC authorization adapter: User -> Role Collection -> Role -> Scope.

OAuth token acquisition, destination handling, and generic HTTP transport are reused from the provisioning solution described in the companion article. The additional logic required for SoD analysis begins with reading the user's assigned role collections.

3.1 Reading the user's role collections

3.1.1 Find User

The adapter first locates the BTP user by username and identity-provider origin. This is the user-to-role-collection entry point.

GET /Users?filter=userName eq "<name>" and origin eq "<origin>"
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json

Representative SCIM response:

{
  "Resources": [
    {
      "id": "8f5c2d10-....",
      "userName": "T_BTPGRC",
      "origin": "sap.default",
      "groups": [
        {
          "value": "4a1b2c3d-....",
          "display": "ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS",
          "type": "DIRECT"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "totalResults": 1
}

The filter is URL-encoded. The adapter consumes the identity fields and, most importantly, groups[*]. Each group represents an assigned role collection; display is the collection name and value is its identifier.

3.1.2 List Users

GRC calls this operation when it enumerates users for the connector:

GET /Users?count=1000&attributes=id,userName,origin,name,active,verified,emails
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json

Representative response:

{
  "Resources": [
    {
      "id": "8f5c2d10-....",
      "userName": "T_BTPGRC",
      "origin": "sap.default",
      "active": true,
      "verified": true,
      "emails": []
    }
  ],
  "totalResults": 1
}

 

3.2 Reading role collections, roles, and scopes

3.2.1 List Role Collections

The adapter enumerates role collections through the SCIM Groups endpoint. This supports GRC's role-list operation:

GET /Groups?startIndex=1&count=100&attributes=id,displayName
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json

Representative response:

{
  "Resources": [
    {
      "id": "4a1b2c3d-....",
      "displayName": "ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS"
    }
  ],
  "totalResults": 1
}

The client follows the SCIM pagination fields and requests subsequent pages until all role collections have been retrieved. The result is then sorted by displayName, and GRC exposes one row per role collection.

3.2.2 Get User Role Collections

The adapter obtains a user's role collection assignments from the groups attribute in the SCIM user response. Internally, get_role_collections_for_user( ) calls find_user_by_username( ), which performs the lookup using the user's username and identity-provider origin:

GET /Users?filter=userName eq "T_BTPGRC" and origin eq "sap.default"
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json
{
  "userName": "T_BTPGRC",
  "origin": "sap.default",
  "groups": [
    {
      "value": "4a1b2c3d-....",
      "display": "ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS",
      "type": "DIRECT"
    }
  ]
}

For each entry in groups[*], display is mapped to the role collection name used for the Authorization v2 lookup, while value is retained as the SCIM group identifier. The adapter skips entries with a blank display, sorts the remaining entries by role-collection name, and removes duplicate names before continuing to role-collection detail retrieval.

3.2.3 Get Role Collection Detail

The Authorization v2 endpoint resolves a role collection into its concrete role references:

GET /sap/rest/authorization/v2/rolecollections/<name-url-encoded>
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/json

Representative response:

{
  "name": "ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS",
  "description": "General user access",
  "role_references": [
    {
      "app_id": "aicore!b164",
      "template_name": "aicore_batch_admin",
      "role_name": "aicore_batch_admin"
    }
  ]
}

Results are cached for the duration of the risk-analysis request.

3.2.4 Get Role Detail and Scopes

For every role reference, the adapter reads the concrete role and its scopes:

GET /sap/rest/authorization/v2/apps/<app>/roletemplates/<template>/roles/<role>
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/json

Representative response:

{
  "app_id": "aicore!b164",
  "template_name": "aicore_batch_admin",
  "name": "aicore_batch_admin",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.read" },
    { "name": "aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write" }
  ]
}

The adapter extracts scopes[*].name (or scope_name for a schema variant). A missing role is treated as an empty scope list and cached keyed by app_id | template | role_name. Other API or communication errors are handled separately and are not interpreted as empty authorization data.

The resulting read chain is: User -> Role Collection -> Role -> Scope

3.3 Flattening the Authorization Chain

For SoD analysis, the client expands the chain into one row per scope, tagged with the role collection, application, role template, and concrete role that grant it:

User
         -> Role Collection
                   -> Role
                             -> Scope

Apart from basic GET methods, we have additional methods expand_user_scopes( ) and expand_role_collection_scopes( ) in class ZCL_BTP_XSUAA_CLIENT  which help flatten the authorization chain into scope rows for the adapter.
For example, assume user T_BTPGRC is assigned to the role collection ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS, which contains the role aicore_batch_admin. The adapter can expand the authorizations from either entry point:

expand_user_scopes( 'T_BTPGRC' )
  -> ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS
      -> aicore_batch_admin
          -> aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.read
          -> aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write

expand_role_collection_scopes( 'ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS' )
  -> aicore_batch_admin
      -> aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.read
      -> aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write

 

3.4 Scope Structure and Parsing

BTP scopes are xsappname.object.path.verb. Splitting must happen on the last dot so multi-segment object paths (aicore!b164.scenarios.batches) survive intact. The client preserves the complete BTP scope and splits it on the final period:
object = aicore!b164.scenarios.batches
verb = write

This keeps multi-segment paths intact. The parser's essential behavior is:

METHOD parse_scope_to_obj_actvt.
  CLEAR: ev_object, ev_actvt.
  DATA(lv_len) = strlen( iv_scope ).
  DATA(lv_pos) = lv_len.
  WHILE lv_pos > 0.
    lv_pos = lv_pos - 1.
    IF substring( val = iv_scope off = lv_pos len = 1 ) = '.'.
      ev_object = substring( val = iv_scope off = 0 len = lv_pos ).
      ev_actvt  = substring( val = iv_scope off = lv_pos + 1 len = lv_len - lv_pos - 1 ).
      RETURN.
    ENDIF.
  ENDWHILE.
  ev_object = iv_scope.   " no dot => whole thing is object, actvt blank
ENDMETHOD.

 

Role CollectionApplicationRoleScopeObjectActivity
ZTEMP_BUILD_APPSaicore!b164aicore_batch_adminaicore!b164.scenarios.batches.readaicore!b164.scenarios.batchesread
ZTEMP_BUILD_APPSaicore!b164aicore_batch_adminaicore!b164.scenarios.batches.writeaicore!b164.scenarios.batcheswrite

 

4. The Adapter - ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP

IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT provides the following methods that are essential for risk analysis:

Interface method
GET_USER_LIST
GET_USER_RANGES
GET_ROLE_LIST
GET_ROLE_RANGES
GET_USER_ROLE
GET_USER_RESOURCE
GET_ROLE_RESOURCE
EOM_FOR_REQUEST

Per-instance client caching:

DATA mo_client    TYPE REF TO zcl_btp_xsuaa_client.
DATA mv_last_dest TYPE rfcdest.

METHOD get_client.
  DATA lv_dest TYPE rfcdest.
  lv_dest = iv_dest.
  IF mo_client IS INITIAL OR mv_last_dest <> lv_dest.
    mo_client    = zcl_btp_xsuaa_client=>create_from_connector( iv_connector = lv_dest ).
    mv_last_dest = lv_dest.
  ENDIF.
  ro_client = mo_client.
ENDMETHOD.

One OAuth token and shared caches serve all GET_* calls of a single risk-analysis request. At the end of the risk-analysis request, EOM_FOR_REQUEST clears the request-specific client state and cached authorization data.

4.1. Mapping BTP Scopes to GRC Authorization Rows

Called from both GET_USER_RESOURCE and GET_ROLE_RESOURCE, this turns a single flattened scope row into what the SoD engine will consume. Two output rows are emitted per scope (see §5 for why):

EMIT_SCOPE_ROW( ) is a private helper method in the custom adapter class ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP. It is not a method supplied by SAP. The BTP client retrieves and flattens the authorization data. This helper performs the final mapping into the structures expected by the standard GRC AC risk-analysis engine.

The standard engine reaches this method through the adapter's implementation of IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT:

IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT~GET_USER_RESOURCE
  -> ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP->EMIT_SCOPE_ROW( )

IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT~GET_ROLE_RESOURCE
  -> ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP->EMIT_SCOPE_ROW( )

Both callers pass one flattened TY_SCOPE_ROW from ZCL_BTP_XSUAA_CLIENT. The row contains the role collection, role, complete BTP scope, parsed object, and activity. The helper also receives the resource and role exclusion ranges supplied by GRC, and returns its results through the changing tables CT_SODAUTHS and CT_ROLES.

The method performs three tasks:

  1. It ignores incomplete scopes, including scopes without an activity suffix, and skips roles excluded by the GRC analysis request.
  2. It creates a permission-level authorization row using SCOPE / ACTVT, with the BTP verb in FROMVAL.
  3. It creates a second, shadow action-level row using S_TCODE / TCD, with the BTP object in FROMVAL, and records the role-to-role-collection relationship in CT_ROLES.

The two authorization rows allow the same BTP scope to participate in both permission-level and action-level SoD analysis (see §5 for why the shadow row is required):

EMIT_SCOPE_ROW( ) example for scope aicore!b164.scenarios.batches.write

Output tableROLERESOURCEIDRESOURCEEXTNFROMVALOther relevant field
CT_SODAUTHSaicore_batch_adminS_TCODETCDaicore!b164.scenarios.batchesPRMSOURCE = ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS
CT_SODAUTHSaicore_batch_adminSCOPEACTVTwritePRMSOURCE = ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS
CT_ROLESaicore_batch_admin---COMPROLE = ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS

The first row deliberately uses the standard S_TCODE / TCD resource so action-level analysis can find the BTP object. The second row is the BTP-native permission representation (SCOPE & ACTVT) used by permission level analysis. The role relationship lets GRC retain the fact that aicore_batch_admin was delivered through the ZTEMP_BUILD_APPS role collection.

5. Why the adapter emits a shadow action row

Standard class CL_GRAC_SOD_RISK_ANALYSIS->LOAD_OBJ_AUTH_SYSTEM reads the sodauths we emitted and routes each row into one of these internal buckets by a hardcoded whitelist of resourceid / resourceextn constants namely S_TCODE, S_START, S_SERVICE, etc.

The action-level analysis paths (MATCH_ACTRULE_TO_AUTHS) only look inside singleaction. Any BTP-native resourceid like SCOPE gets routed to others and is invisible to action-level SoD.

Therefore, for every scope we emit two rows - a real permission row (SCOPE/ ACTVT) and a shadow action row (S_TCODE/ TCD) whose fromval is the scope object which satisfies both action level and permission level risk analysis.

 

6. Extending the SoD ruleset with BTP authorization data

BTP native resourceids are not maintained on standard GRACFUNCPRM / GRACFUNCACT. Because our connector has GRACCONNECTOR-EXTOBJ_ENABLED = 'X', the engine picks up the extended tables GRACFUNCPRMEXT / GRACFUNCACTEXT instead (config parameter 1046). The following example shows the risk configured in the ruleset.

Example of function configuration: FUNC1

Functions representation at table level

Note the design: RESOURCEID = SCOPE  is a constant (is an identifier and can be given any name), and the scope object goes into ACTION. This mirrors what the adapter emits in the permission row.

 

7. The Result - Risk Analysis

The integration was validated through standalone user-level and access-request risk analyses. In both scenarios, the custom adapter retrieved the relevant BTP role collections, roles, and scopes, mapped them to GRC authorization rows, and enabled the standard GRC risk-analysis engine to identify the configured risks.

User level standalone RA:

Access request RA:

 

8. Conclusion

This integration demonstrates that SAP GRC Access Control can remain the central governance, approval, and risk-analysis layer even when the target access is hosted in SAP BTP. By using the standard IF_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT extension point, the solution brings XSUAA users, role collections, roles, and scopes into the existing GRC process without modifying the core SoD engine.

The key design element is the custom authorization adapter and its BTP client. Together, they translate SCIM and Authorization v2 API responses into the structures expected by GRC, preserve BTP-native scope values, and emit both permission-level and action-level authorization rows.

For production use, the implementation should be strengthened with secure OAuth credential handling, least-privilege API scopes, controlled destination configuration, reliable user and role-collection synchronization, monitoring, and clear operational error handling. With these controls in place, this approach provides a practical and reusable bridge between SAP GRC Access Control governance and SAP BTP XSUAA authorization.

 

9. References

  1. https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/cp-sapcp-getstarted.html
  2. https://api.sap.com/api/PlatformAPI/overview

entry.title: Securing SAP Cloud Integration iFlows Using Custom User Roles and System-Specific Credentials
entry.content:
Introduction

Modern enterprise landscapes often rely on SAP Integration Suite to connect SAP applications with a diverse set of business and third-party applications, including CRM, e-commerce, logistics, HR, banking, business intelligence, and industry-specific platforms.

In one of our integration scenarios, we had multiple external applications communicating with SAP Cloud Integration. For this article, the systems are anonymized as the BI System, CRM System, and WMS System. Each application had its own business purpose and its own set of integration flows.

The customer had a specific security requirement: credentials issued to one application should not be reusable to invoke integration flows belonging to another application.

The requirement was: BI credentials should be able to invoke BI-related iFlows, but should not be usable to invoke CRM or WMS iFlows.

This requirement made us look beyond authentication alone. We needed an authorization boundary between the applications. We therefore implemented a system-specific User Role model, where each application has its own custom role and corresponding service-instance credentials.

This blog explains an approach to achieve system/application-specific authorization by creating dedicated roles in SAP Cloud Integration and using those roles for the corresponding iFlows and BTP service keys.

The key principle is consistency: the role configured for the service instance must match the role configured for the iFlow.

The Customer Scenario
The integration landscape contained three application domains:

Application

Example iFlows

Required Access

BI System

BI_to_SAP

BI flows only

CRM System

CRM_to_SAP

CRM flows only

WMS System

WMS_to_SAP

WMS flows only

BI credentials → BI custom role → BI iFlows
CRM credentials → CRM custom role → CRM iFlows
WMS credentials → WMS custom role → WMS iFlows

What Was the Problem?
The challenge was not simply to provide different client credentials. The customer also wanted those credentials to represent different authorization boundaries.

The predefined ESBMessaging.send role is available for inbound integration flow processing. For our scenario, however, the customer wanted a more explicit application-level separation. We therefore created separate custom User Roles and used the same role consistently between the BTP service instance and the corresponding iFlow sender adapter.

BI System → BI Service Key → ESBMessaging_BI → BI iFlows
CRM System → CRM Service Key → ESBMessaging_CRM → CRM iFlows
WMS System → WMS Service Key → ESBMessaging_WMS → WMS iFlows

The Approach We Implemented

  1. Create a dedicated custom User Role for each application.
  2. Configure the same custom role in the sender adapter of the relevant iFlows.
  3. Create an SAP Process Integration Runtime service instance for the application.
  4. Configure the service instance with the application's custom role.
  5. Create a service key from that service instance.
  6. Test both the authorized and unauthorized paths.

High-Level Architecture
The overall approach can be visualized as follows:

The key design principle is that the same role is used on both sides of the authorization relationship: the BTP service instance/service key and the iFlow sender adapter.

 

Step 1 – Create a Custom User Role

Navigate to the Manage Security section in SAP Integration Suite and open User Roles. Select Add and provide a role name and description.

For the BI System, we use the following custom role:
ESBMessaging_BI

Following the same naming convention, the other applications can use:
ESBMessaging_CRM
ESBMessaging_WMS



Once created, the custom roles becomes available in the User Roles list.

 

Step 2 – Assign the Role to the Relevant iFlows

Once the custom role has been created, configure the sender adapter of the relevant iFlow to use User Role authorization and select the corresponding application-specific role.

BI iFlows → Authorization: User Role → ESBMessaging_BI
CRM iFlows → Authorization: User Role → ESBMessaging_CRM
WMS iFlows → Authorization: User Role → ESBMessaging_WMS

 

Step 3 – Create the BTP Service Instance

The next step is to create a dedicated service Instance in SAP BTP for the corresponding application.
Navigate to the SAP BTP subaccount and open Instances and Subscriptions. Select the Instances tab and choose Create.

In the Basic Info step, provide the required values:

Parameter

Value / Example

Service

SAP Process Integration Runtime

Plan

integration-flow

Runtime Environment

Cloud Foundry

Space

Appropriate space

Instance Name

Unique application-specific instance name

Click Next.

 

Step 4 – Assign the Custom Role to the Service Instance

In the service instance configuration, remove the default role and add the custom role created for the application.

For the BI System, the relevant configuration is:

{
    "roles": [
        "ESBMessaging_BI"
    ],
    "grant-types": [
        "client_credentials"
    ],
    "redirect-uris": [
    ],
    "token-validity": 3600
}

The important part of the configuration is the roles property. The role assigned here must match the role configured in the BI iFlow sender adapter.

 

Step 5 – Create the Service Key

From the created service instance, open the Actions menu (three dots) and select Create Service Key. Enter a service key name and create the key.




After creation, the service key is available under the service instance. The credentials can then be provided to the corresponding application.

Follow the same steps for the other two applications to create the service instances and service keys, and assign the appropriate roles.

 

Step 6 – Test the Integration

Once the iFlow is deployed, use the service key credentials to invoke the integration endpoint from a client such as Postman.

Test 1 – Correct Credentials Against the Correct iFlow

The first test validates the expected authorization path. BI credentials are used to invoke the BI iFlow.

BI Credentials
↓
ESBMessaging_BI
↓
BI iFlow
↓
Request is authorized
↓
Integration flow executes

This returned 200 success code.
This confirms that the service key, custom role, and iFlow sender configuration are aligned.

Test 2 – BI Credentials Against Another Application's iFlow

The second test is the critical negative test. We deliberately use the BI System credentials to invoke an iFlow protected by another application's role, for example a CRM iFlow.

BI Credentials
↓
ESBMessaging_BI
↓
CRM iFlow
↓
CRM role required
↓
Request is rejected

This returned 401 unauthorized error code.
This confirms that the system call is rejected.

 

Why This Approach Is Useful

This approach provides several benefits.

Application-Level Isolation
Each application gets its own authorization boundary.
This reduces the possibility of one application's credentials being used to access another application's integrations.

Better Security Governance
Instead of having a common authorization model for all external systems, each application can have its own role.

For example:

BI Application → Role ESBMessaging_BI
CRM Application → Role ESBMessaging_CRM
WMS Application → Role ESBMessaging_WMS

This makes security ownership easier to understand.

Easier Credential Management
If credentials for one application need to be rotated or revoked, the change can be handled within that application's security boundary.

For example:

BI System credentials compromised
        |
        v
Revoke/rotate BI System credentials
        |
        v
CRM System and WMS System remain isolated

Reduced Blast Radius
A major security principle is to reduce the impact of a compromised credential.

If every external application uses the same credentials/authorization, a compromise could potentially affect multiple integrations.

With system-specific authorization, the intended blast radius is reduced to the relevant application and its integrations.

 

Conclusion

When multiple applications are integrated with SAP Cloud Integration, using a common authorization model can make it difficult to enforce application-level isolation.

A system-specific role approach provides a way to establish separate authorization boundaries for different applications.

The most important part of the implementation is not only creating separate credentials, but also ensuring that the corresponding authorization is restricted to the intended integration flows.

Finally, always validate the implementation with both positive and negative authorization tests:

Correct Application → Allowed ✅

Wrong Application → Denied ❌

This provides a practical way to implement the principle of least privilege for applications consuming SAP Cloud Integration iFlows.

By applying this pattern consistently, organizations can build a more structured and manageable inbound authorization model for integrations between SAP Cloud Integration and multiple external applications.

entry.title: How I Enabled Support of bot Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application
entry.content:
Supporting Standalone and Managed Approuters in One SAPUI5 and SAP CAP Application

Introduction

While developing an SAPUI5 application on SAP BTP, I encountered a requirement that initially appeared straightforward:

  • The application should be directly accessible through a standalone approuter.
  • The same application should also be available through SAP Build Work Zone using its managed approuter.
  • Both entry points should use the same SAPUI5 codebase and SAP CAP backend.
  • Authentication, authorization, and OData communication should work consistently in both environments.

The application worked correctly when accessed through the standalone approuter. However, when I opened the same application from SAP Build Work Zone, I started encountering HTTP 404 errors, authentication failures, incorrect OData paths, and Content Security Policy issues with SAPUI5 VizFrame charts.

I initially assumed that because both runtime models use an xs-app.json file, the same routing configuration and absolute OData URLs would work in both environments. I eventually discovered that this assumption was incorrect.

The standalone and managed approuters serve the application from different URL contexts. This seemingly small difference directly affects how frontend service URLs are resolved.

In this article, I explain the architecture I designed and developed to support both approuter models using:

  • A single SAPUI5 codebase
  • A single SAP CAP service
  • XSUAA-based authentication
  • User-token propagation
  • SAP Destination service
  • HTML5 Application Repository
  • SAP Build Work Zone
  • Separate routing configurations
  • Runtime-aware OData URL resolution

This article is based on a real implementation and includes the design decisions, dead ends, configuration, code, and troubleshooting lessons from that experience.

The problem I was trying to solve

The application needed to support two access patterns.

Direct application access

Users should be able to open the application through a dedicated Cloud Foundry route exposed by a standalone approuter.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
Standalone Approuter
   |
   +---- Serves the SAPUI5 application
   |
   +---- Forwards OData requests
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

SAP Build Work Zone access

The same application should be available as an SAP Fiori application inside SAP Build Work Zone.

The request flow should be:

Browser
   |
   v
SAP Build Work Zone
   |
   v
Managed Approuter
   |
   +---- Loads the application from the HTML5 Application Repository
   |
   +---- Resolves the backend destination
   |
   v
SAP CAP Service

I wanted to avoid maintaining separate SAPUI5 applications or separate frontend builds for these two environments.

The first issue I encountered

My application initially used root-relative OData paths:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

This worked correctly through the standalone approuter because the application and the OData route were available from the same host root.

For example:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

However, the managed approuter uses an application-specific prefix when serving an application from the HTML5 Application Repository.

A simplified managed-approuter URL can look like this:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/index.html

The corresponding OData request may need to retain that prefix:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

When I used a leading slash:

/odata/v4/my-service/

the browser resolved the request from the host root and discarded the application prefix.

The request therefore became:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/odata/v4/my-service/

instead of:

https://<managed-approuter-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

This resulted in an HTTP 404 response.

The most surprising part of the investigation was that a single leading slash determined whether the application worked or failed. Because the same URL worked through the standalone approuter, I initially investigated destination configuration and XSUAA authorization instead of URL resolution.

The design decision

I considered using environment-specific service URLs:

if (managedApprouter) {
    // Use managed-approuter URL
} else {
    // Use standalone-approuter URL
}

Another option was to maintain separate frontend builds for each runtime.

I decided against both approaches because they would:

  • Duplicate configuration
  • Introduce environment-specific code
  • Make deployments harder to maintain
  • Increase the risk of one version behaving differently from the other
  • Require changes whenever an application name or route changed

Instead, I designed a URL resolver that derives the service URL from the SAPUI5 component’s actual runtime location.

This allows the application to preserve the managed-approuter prefix while still supporting local CAP execution and the standalone approuter.

Project structure

The relevant project structure is:

project-root/
|
|-- app/
|   |
|   |-- my-ui5-app/
|       |
|       |-- webapp/
|       |   |-- controller/
|       |   |-- model/
|       |   |   |-- serviceUrl.js
|       |   |-- Component.js
|       |   |-- manifest.json
|       |   |-- index.html
|       |
|       |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- router/
|   |-- package.json
|   |-- xs-app.json
|
|-- srv/
|   |-- service.cds
|   |-- service.js
|
|-- xs-security.json
|-- mta.yaml
|-- package.json

Two xs-app.json files are intentionally maintained:

  • router/xs-app.json configures the standalone approuter.
  • app/my-ui5-app/xs-app.json configures the managed-approuter runtime.

Although the files have similar backend routes, they serve frontend content differently.

Standalone approuter implementation

Standalone approuter package

The standalone approuter is a Node.js Cloud Foundry application using @SAP/approuter.

The router/package.json can be defined as follows:

{
  "name": "my-standalone-approuter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/approuter": "^20.0.0"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js"
  }
}

The approuter itself does not contain application business logic. It handles responsibilities such as:

  • User authentication
  • Route matching
  • Forwarding requests
  • Token propagation
  • Serving frontend resources

Standalone xs-app.json

The standalone approuter serves the SAPUI5 application from its local webapp directory and forwards OData requests to the SAP CAP service.

{
  "welcomeFile": "index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "localDir": "webapp",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

OData route

The following route captures requests beginning with /odata/:

{
  "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
  "target": "/odata/$1",
  "destination": "srv-api",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "csrfProtection": false
}

For example:

/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

is forwarded to:

<srv-api>/odata/v4/my-service/Requests

Frontend route

The final route serves the SAPUI5 files:

{
  "source": "^/(.*)$",
  "localDir": "webapp",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
  "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
}

This works because the standalone approuter module contains a copy of the built SAPUI5 webapp content.

Managed approuter implementation

In the managed-approuter scenario, I did not serve the frontend from the standalone router’s local directory.

Instead:

  1. The SAPUI5 application is built.
  2. The application is packaged as a ZIP archive.
  3. The archive is uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository.
  4. SAP Build Work Zone discovers the application.
  5. The managed approuter loads it from the repository.
  6. Backend requests are forwarded through a destination.

Managed xs-app.json

The managed-approuter configuration belongs to the HTML5 application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/index.html",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/api-docs(.*)$",
      "target": "/api-docs$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/odata/(.*)$",
      "target": "/odata/$1",
      "destination": "srv-api",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^(.*)$",
      "target": "$1",
      "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "cacheControl": "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"
    }
  ]
}

The important difference is the frontend route:

{
  "source": "^(.*)$",
  "target": "$1",
  "service": "html5-apps-repo-rt",
  "authenticationType": "xsuaa"
}

Instead of using:

"localDir": "webapp"

the managed approuter loads the application through:

"service": "html5-apps-repo-rt"

This distinction is fundamental.

Runtime Frontend source
Standalone approuterLocal application directory
Managed approuterHTML5 Application Repository runtime

Dynamic OData URL resolution

The key part of my design was to stop treating the OData endpoint as a fixed root-relative URL.

Instead of this:

const SERVICE_URL = "/odata/v4/my-service/";

I used a relative service path:

const SERVICE_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

I then introduced a reusable SAPUI5 URL-resolution module.

serviceUrl.js

sap.ui.define([], () => {
    "use strict";

    const LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH = /\/my-ui5-app(?:\/webapp)?\/?$/;

    function resolve(sUri) {
        const sRelativeUri = String(sUri || "").replace(/^\/+/, "");

        const oComponentBaseUrl = new URL(
            sap.ui.require.toUrl("my/ui5/app/"),
            window.location.href
        );

        /*
         * During local CAP execution, the UI may be served below:
         *
         * /my-ui5-app/webapp
         *
         * while the CAP OData service is exposed from:
         *
         * /odata
         */
        if (LOCAL_CAP_APP_PATH.test(oComponentBaseUrl.pathname)) {
            return new URL(
                `/${sRelativeUri}`,
                oComponentBaseUrl.origin
            ).toString();
        }

        /*
         * For a managed approuter, retain the HTML5 application
         * prefix by resolving the path relative to the component.
         */
        return new URL(
            sRelativeUri,
            oComponentBaseUrl
        ).toString();
    }

    return {
        resolve
    };
});

Replace the following values with your application-specific values:

/my-ui5-app/

and:

"my/ui5/app/"

The namespace should correspond to the SAPUI5 application namespace.

Why this resolver works

Local CAP runtime

Suppose the application is served locally from:

http://localhost:4004/my-ui5-app/webapp/

The resolver recognizes the local CAP application path and produces:

http://localhost:4004/odata/v4/my-service/

Standalone approuter

Suppose the application is served from:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/

The service URL resolves to:

https://my-standalone-router.example.com/odata/v4/my-service/

Managed approuter

Suppose the SAPUI5 component is served from:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/

The relative service path resolves to:

https://<managed-host>/<application-prefix>/odata/v4/my-service/

The managed-approuter application prefix remains intact.

Using the resolver in the SAPUI5 application

The service constants should not start with /:

const SERVICE_V2_URL = "odata/v2/my-service/";
const SERVICE_V4_URL = "odata/v4/my-service/";

The resolver can then be imported into a controller or component.

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/UIComponent",
    "my/ui5/app/model/serviceUrl"
], function (
    UIComponent,
    serviceUrl
) {
    "use strict";

    return UIComponent.extend("my.ui5.app.Component", {
        metadata: {
            manifest: "json"
        },

        init: function () {
            UIComponent.prototype.init.apply(this, arguments);

            const sServiceUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
                "odata/v4/my-service/"
            );

            console.log("Resolved service URL:", sServiceUrl);

            this.getRouter().initialize();
        }
    });
});

It can also be used for direct fetch calls:

const sUrl = serviceUrl.resolve(
    "odata/v4/my-service/getDashboardData"
);

fetch(sUrl, {
    method: "GET",
    credentials: "include",
    headers: {
        "Accept": "application/json"
    }
})
    .then(function (oResponse) {
        if (!oResponse.ok) {
            throw new Error(
                `Request failed with status ${oResponse.status}`
            );
        }

        return oResponse.json();
    })
    .then(function (oData) {
        console.log(oData);
    });

XSUAA authentication configuration

The application uses XSUAA for user authentication and role-based authorization.

A simplified xs-security.json can look like this:

{
  "xsappname": "my-application",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User",
      "description": "Application user access"
    },
    {
      "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator access"
    }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    {
      "name": "User",
      "description": "Application user",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User"
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Admin",
      "description": "Application administrator",
      "scope-references": [
        "$XSAPPNAME.User",
        "$XSAPPNAME.Admin"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

After deployment:

  1. Create the required role collections.
  2. Add the generated role templates.
  3. Assign the role collections to the relevant users or identity-provider groups.

A successful login only confirms that the identity provider authenticated the user. It does not automatically mean that the user has every application scope.

MTA configuration

The MTA contains the following major components:

SAP CAP service
Standalone approuter
SAPUI5 HTML5 module
HTML5 application content deployer
Destination content module
XSUAA service
Destination service
HTML5 repository host
HTML5 repository runtime

The following excerpts show the important relationships.

SAP CAP service module

modules:
  - name: my-application-srv
    type: nodejs
    path: gen/srv

    provides:
      - name: srv-api
        properties:
          srv-url: ${default-url}

    requires:
      - name: my-application-auth

    parameters:
      buildpack: nodejs_buildpack
      memory: 512M

The service exposes its runtime URL through the srv-api dependency:

provides:
  - name: srv-api
    properties:
      srv-url: ${default-url}

Standalone approuter module

  - name: my-application-router
    type: approuter.nodejs
    path: gen/router

    requires:
      - name: srv-api
        group: destinations
        properties:
          name: srv-api
          url: ~{srv-url}
          forwardAuthToken: true

      - name: my-application-auth

      - name: my-application-destination

      - name: my-application-html5-runtime

The following configuration propagates the logged-in user’s token to the CAP service:

forwardAuthToken: true

Without token forwarding, the CAP service may receive an anonymous or technically incomplete request and return HTTP 401 or 403.

SAPUI5 HTML5 module

  - name: my-ui5-app
    type: html5
    path: app/my-ui5-app

    build-parameters:
      builder: custom
      commands:
        - npm ci
        - npm run build
      supported-platforms: []
      build-result: dist

HTML5 application deployer

  - name: my-application-app-content
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .

    requires:
      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          content-target: true

    build-parameters:
      build-result: resources
      requires:
        - name: my-ui5-app
          artifacts:
            - my-ui5-app.zip
          target-path: resources/

This module uploads the built SAPUI5 application to the HTML5 Application Repository.

Destination content module

  - name: my-application-destination-content
    type: com.sap.application.content

    requires:
      - name: my-application-destination
        parameters:
          content-target: true

      - name: my-application-html5-host
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-html5-host-key

      - name: my-application-auth
        parameters:
          service-key:
            name: my-application-auth-key

      - name: srv-api

    parameters:
      content:
        instance:
          destinations:
            - Name: srv-api
              Type: HTTP
              ProxyType: Internet
              URL: ~{srv-api/srv-url}
              Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange
              HTML5.DynamicDestination: true
              HTML5.ForwardAuthToken: true

          existing_destinations_policy: update

For the managed-approuter flow, I used:

Authentication: OAuth2UserTokenExchange

This allows the destination to exchange and propagate the logged-in user’s security context when calling the protected CAP service.

Required resources

resources:
  - name: my-application-auth
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application
      path: ./xs-security.json

  - name: my-application-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite
      config:
        HTML5Runtime_enabled: true

  - name: my-application-html5-host
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-host

  - name: my-application-html5-runtime
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-runtime

Connecting the application to SAP Build Work Zone

The SAPUI5 manifest.json should contain the appropriate sap.cloud configuration:

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "my.ui5.app",
    "type": "application",
    "applicationVersion": {
      "version": "1.0.0"
    }
  },
  "sap.cloud": {
    "public": true,
    "service": "my.application.service"
  }
}

The same sap.cloud.service value must be used consistently in the destination content where applicable.

For example:

sap.cloud.service: my.application.service

I found that a mismatch here could make the deployment succeed while preventing the application from being discovered or resolved correctly in the Work Zone content provider.

After deployment:

  1. Open SAP Build Work Zone administration.
  2. Open the Channel Manager or content provider configuration.
  3. Refresh the HTML5 Apps content provider.
  4. Add the application to My Content.
  5. Assign it to a role.
  6. Add it to a workspace, page, or site.
  7. Ensure the user has the corresponding Work Zone role assignment and XSUAA role collection.

Content Security Policy and VizFrame

After solving the OData routing problem, I encountered another issue: the reports page worked in SAP Build Work Zone, but the charts failed through the standalone approuter.

The browser console displayed an error similar to:

Creating a worker from 'blob:...' violates the following
Content Security Policy directive: "script-src ..."

It also displayed:

Failed to construct 'Worker'

I initially investigated the VizFrame chart configuration because the chart controls were not rendering. However, the chart data and bindings were correct.

The actual problem was that the visualization library attempted to create a web worker using a blob: URL, but the application’s Content Security Policy did not allow it.

I updated the CSP in index.html:

<meta
    http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
    content="
        default-src 'self';
        script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        worker-src 'self' blob:;
        style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        font-src 'self' data:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        img-src 'self' data: blob:
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
        connect-src 'self'
            https://sapui5.hana.ondemand.com;
    "
/>

The important addition was:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

The final CSP should be reviewed according to the organization’s security requirements. Permissions such as 'unsafe-eval' should not be added automatically unless required by the selected SAPUI5 version or application behavior and accepted by the relevant security team.

CSRF protection

The routing examples in this article show:

"csrfProtection": false

This reflects the implementation being discussed, but it should not be interpreted as a recommendation to disable CSRF protection for every route.

For state-changing OData requests, such as:

  • POST
  • PATCH
  • PUT
  • DELETE

the safer approach is to use the OData model’s built-in CSRF handling or explicitly fetch and send a CSRF token.

For example:

X-CSRF-Token: Fetch

The selected approach should be aligned with:

  • The CAP service behavior
  • The SAPUI5 OData model
  • The application’s authentication model
  • Organizational security standards
  • Whether the endpoint is read-only or state-changing

Building and deploying the application

Install the project dependencies:

npm install

Build the CAP project:

npx cds build --production

Build the MTA archive:

mbt build

Log in to the target Cloud Foundry environment:

cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Select the correct organization and space:

cf target -o "<organization>" -s "<space>"

Deploy the MTA archive:

cf deploy mta_archives/<archive-name>.mtar

After deployment, verify the application through both entry points.

Standalone approuter

https://<standalone-approuter-route>/

Managed approuter

Open the application through SAP Build Work Zone or the relevant HTML5 application runtime entry point.

Troubleshooting lessons from my implementation

HTTP 404 for OData requests only in SAP Build Work Zone

Symptom

The UI loads, but the OData request returns HTTP 404.

What I initially assumed

I initially treated this as a missing destination or incorrect backend route.

Actual cause

The OData request used a root-relative URL:

/odata/v4/my-service/

This removed the managed-approuter application prefix.

Resolution

Use a component-relative path:

odata/v4/my-service/

and resolve it against the SAPUI5 component location.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized

Possible causes
