  • Missing or invalid XSUAA binding
  • Expired authentication session
  • Missing token propagation
  • Destination using the wrong authentication method
  • Direct access to the CAP service instead of access through the approuter

Important lesson

An HTTP 401 response does not always mean the role configuration is wrong. I learned to inspect the complete request URL first.

If the request reached the wrong route because its application prefix was missing, changing scopes or role collections would not solve the problem.

HTTP 403 Forbidden

Possible causes

  • The user is authenticated but lacks the required scope
  • The correct role collection was not assigned
  • The destination propagated a technical token instead of the user token
  • The CAP authorization annotation rejected the user
  • Application-level user provisioning rejected the user

Difference between 401 and 403

A simplified interpretation is:

401: The request does not have acceptable authentication.
403: The identity is known, but it does not have permission.

Application works through Work Zone but not through the standalone approuter

Check the following:

  • Does the standalone approuter contain the built webapp content?
  • Does router/xs-app.json use localDir?
  • Is the standalone approuter bound to XSUAA?
  • Is the srv-api destination injected?
  • Is forwardAuthToken enabled?
  • Is the frontend route placed after the more specific OData routes?

Route order matters because the generic frontend route can otherwise capture requests intended for the backend.

Application works through the standalone approuter but not through Work Zone

Check the following:

  • Was the SAPUI5 ZIP uploaded to the HTML5 Application Repository?
  • Does the HTML5 application contain its own xs-app.json?
  • Is HTML5Runtime_enabled set correctly?
  • Does the destination exist?
  • Does the destination name exactly match srv-api?
  • Is sap.cloud.service consistent?
  • Was the Work Zone content provider refreshed?
  • Was the application assigned to the required role and site?
  • Does the OData URL preserve the managed-approuter application prefix?

Charts fail only in one runtime

Open the browser console and look for:

Content Security Policy

or:

Failed to construct Worker

If VizFrame uses a blob worker, verify that the CSP contains:

worker-src 'self' blob:;

This was particularly instructive because the problem appeared to be in the chart implementation, while the actual cause was browser security policy.

Missing i18n files

SAPUI5 may attempt to load locale-specific files such as:

i18n/i18n_en.properties
i18n/i18n_en_GB.properties

If these files are not available, the browser can display HTTP 404 warnings.

Depending on the application’s localization strategy, either create the required files or verify that the fallback bundle is configured correctly.

Architecture summary

The final architecture I implemented can be summarized as follows:

                           +-------------------------+
                           |       SAP CAP Service   |
                           |     Protected by XSUAA  |
                           +------------+------------+
                                        ^
                                        |
                              User token forwarding
                                        |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                  |                                           |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
       | Standalone Approuter |                   |   Managed Approuter   |
       | Cloud Foundry App    |                   | SAP Build Work Zone   |
       +----------+-----------+                   +-----------+-----------+
                  |                                           |
       Local SAPUI5 content                       HTML5 App Repository
                  |                                           |
                  +---------------------+---------------------+
                                        |
                              Same SAPUI5 codebase

The two runtimes have different routing responsibilities, but they use the same application logic.

What I would do differently next time

Looking back, I would validate the application through both approuter models much earlier in the development cycle.

My initial local and standalone-approuter testing gave me confidence that the routing was complete. However, it did not expose the managed-approuter prefix behavior.

For a future implementation, I would test these scenarios from the beginning:

  1. Local CAP runtime
  2. Standalone approuter
  3. Managed approuter
  4. Direct OData read
  5. State-changing OData request
  6. Role-restricted request
  7. VizFrame or worker-based UI functionality
  8. Session expiry and reauthentication

I would also inspect the final browser request URL before changing destination or authorization configurations. That simple step would have shortened my troubleshooting considerably.

Key takeaways

The most important lesson from this implementation is that supporting both approuter models is not simply a matter of deploying two routers.

The frontend URL strategy, destination configuration, authentication flow, HTML5 application packaging, and runtime routing must all work together.

My main takeaways were:

  • Do not assume identical-looking URLs behave identically across runtime models.
  • Avoid root-relative service URLs when an application may run behind a managed-approuter prefix.
  • Resolve backend URLs relative to the SAPUI5 component.
  • Keep runtime-specific routing configurations separate.
  • Keep the frontend business logic shared.
  • Forward the authenticated user token to protected CAP services.
  • Do not assume every HTTP 401 or 404 response is caused by XSUAA.
  • Verify the complete browser request URL before changing authorization settings.
  • Ensure sap.cloud.service values are consistent.
  • Treat Content Security Policy as part of the application architecture.
  • Test both runtime models early rather than after the application is complete.

The design allowed me to support direct access and SAP Build Work Zone access using one SAPUI5 codebase and one SAP CAP backend, without hard-coded deployment URLs or duplicated frontend applications.

I hope this experience helps other SAP BTP architects and developers who encounter the same routing and authentication challenges.

I would be interested to hear how others have designed applications that need to support both standalone and managed approuters.

entry.title: Building a Modular Utilities Portal for SAP Integration Suite on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Integration teams often build useful scripts and reports for recurring operational tasks. As that collection grows, separate URLs, authentication rules, and deployment processes become difficult to manage. This portal applies a modular pattern: one authenticated entry point presents a consistent experience, and purpose-built services perform the actual work behind protected routes.
The implementation is an example of how SAP BTP can host lightweight tools around SAP Integration Suite without combining every function into one backend. Each module can evolve independently while sharing the same security and release model.


Link to specific App related blogs - 
CPI Artifacts Export to Sharepoint 
Payload Logging and Downloading from SAP DMS

Purpose and project scope

The portal supports design, delivery, and operations activities that are repetitive in a multi-environment Cloud Integration landscape. Its goals are to reduce manual data collection, give users one place to find approved tools, and keep credentials and privileged actions on the server side.

  • Provide one home page for related utilities and their documentation.
  • Apply route-level and backend authorization to each deployed utility.
  • Generate portable outputs such as Excel workbooks, ZIP downloads, DOCX specifications, and SharePoint folders.
  • Allow new utilities to be added as separate modules without rewriting the complete portal.

    Applications in the portal

    Utility

    Purpose

    Primary output

    Status

    Tech Spec Generator

    Creates a technical specification from exported integration content and a Word template. An optional enhanced mode can use a model selected at runtime.

    DOCX

    Available

    Artifacts Status Tracker

    Compares package and artifact deployment status across selected Cloud Integration environments.

    Excel report

    Available

    CPI Artifacts Count

    Counts supported artifact types by package across development, quality, and production environments.

    Excel report

    Available

    DMS Payload Logger

    Searches archived message-processing payloads in SAP Document Management Service and downloads the selected archive.

    ZIP payload

    Available

    CPI Artifact SharePoint Export

    Lists packages from one environment and copies the active versions of selected artifacts to SharePoint Online.

    SharePoint files

    Available

    Mapping Comparator

    Planned workspace for normalizing and comparing baseline and candidate mapping definitions.

    Visual difference report

    Planned

    The Developer Guide is published through the same portal and documents architecture, roles, configuration, deployment, and operations.

    Technical architecture

    The application uses a hub-and-module design. SAP Application Router is the browser-facing entry point. It serves the static user interfaces, starts the XSUAA login flow, checks the scope configured for each route, and forwards API requests to the correct backend destination. The backends validate the forwarded JSON Web Token before processing a request.

    Common process workflow
    1. Authenticate  The user opens the portal and signs in through XSUAA.
    2. Authorize  Application Router checks the route scope, and the backend validates the forwarded token.
    3. Execute  The selected module validates input and calls only the external services required for that function.
    4. Return  The service streams a file or returns display-safe status data to the browser.

      Technical details

      Layer

      Implementation

      User interface

      Static HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript modules. The project does not require React or Next.js.

      Application entry point

      SAP Application Router with route definitions, destination forwarding, logout handling, and XSUAA authentication.

      Backend services

      Node.js services for reporting, DMS access, and artifact export; Python for document generation and deterministic content parsing.

      SAP integrations

      SAP Integration Suite APIs for design-time and runtime data, plus SAP Document Management Service through CMIS-compatible endpoints.

      External integrations

      Microsoft Graph for SharePoint Online upload and an optional OpenAI API connection for enhanced document wording.

      Packaging

      A Multi-Target Application descriptor defines modules, resources, destinations, properties, and service bindings.

      Outputs

      Excel workbooks, Word documents, ZIP payload downloads, JSON manifests, and SharePoint folder structures.

      Security design

      Security is enforced in more than one layer. XSUAA authenticates portal users and provides scopes through role collections. Application Router requires the configured scope before it serves a protected user interface or forwards an API call. Each backend then validates the token and applies any additional standard or administrator permission required by that function.

      • Service credentials are supplied through Cloud Foundry service bindings or user-provided services, not committed to source control.
      • CPI credentials entered for a single operation are kept only for that request or short-lived server job and are not written to browser storage.
      • The SharePoint utility uses delegated Microsoft authorization so file access remains bounded by both the application permission and the signed-in user's access.
      • The optional AI API key remains in the Python backend binding; model discovery and generation requests do not expose it to the browser.
      • Archive uploads and user inputs are validated before parsing or forwarding to an external service.
      Deployment and configuration

      The project is deployed as one MTA to SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. The descriptor creates or references the XSUAA resource, declares the application modules, and binds each backend only to the services it needs. The public example uses placeholders because service instance names, routes, tenant identifiers, client IDs, and secrets differ by landscape.

      Typical service configuration
      • An XSUAA application service for authentication, scopes, and role templates.
      • An SAP Integration Suite API credential binding for reports that use centrally managed credentials.
      • An SAP Document Management Service binding for CMIS search and content download.
      • A user-provided service for Microsoft Entra application settings used by delegated SharePoint access.
      • An optional user-provided service containing the AI API key, bound only to the document-generation backend.
      Practical design considerations
      • Keep the home page simple. Tiles explain purpose and status; routes and backends enforce authorization.
      • Enable multi-step sections only after their prerequisites succeed, as shown in the SharePoint export workflow.
      • Treat external API capabilities as runtime facts and report fallbacks or unsupported cases clearly.
      • Bind each backend only to the DMS, Microsoft, AI, or CPI credential it actually needs.
      Conclusion

      Focused utilities can share one SAP BTP entry point without becoming a tightly coupled application. Application Router and XSUAA provide the common access layer, while separate interfaces and services preserve clear boundaries. The same pattern can support additional tools as integration teams identify repeatable tasks for controlled automation.

entry.title: Minimizing SAP License Costs by optimizing SAP Authorizations with MOON Services

Harness the potential of MOON Services and navigate your way to optimized license management and reduced overhead.

entry.title: Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
Introduction

Many SAP integrations require mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication to securely establish trust between systems. Common scenarios include:

  • SAP S/4HANA outbound integrations
  • Communication arrangements
  • SAP Integration Suite scenarios
  • Partner and third-party API integrations
  • B2B communication channels

To support these scenarios, SAP BTP Destination Service provides a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) capability that can issue client certificates signed by the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy. These certificates are trusted across SAP services and can be used to authenticate outbound calls from SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

This blog walks through the end-to-end UI-based process for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: generating a Certificate Signing Request (CSR), submitting it to SAP BTP Destination Service, and importing the signed certificate back into S/4HANA.

For SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise deployments using STRUST, refer to the companion blog: "Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud".

 

Understanding SAP BTP Destination Service PKI

SAP BTP Destination Service can act as a Certificate Authority service for SAP workloads. It signs Certificate Signing Requests using the SAP Cloud Root CA trust chain, producing certificates that are natively trusted across the SAP ecosystem.

The typical flow is:

  1. Generate a private key and CSR in the target system (S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition)
  2. Upload the CSR to SAP BTP Destination Service
  3. SAP BTP signs the CSR using the SAP Cloud Root CA trust chain
  4. Export the signed certificate chain from BTP Cockpit
  5. Import the signed response back into the target system

Note: The private key never leaves the target system. SAP BTP only receives the CSR and returns a signed certificate chain.

 

API vs UI Approaches

SAP BTP Destination Service supports both API-based and UI-based certificate issuance.

API-Based

UI-Based

The API approach enables automated certificate lifecycle management: submitting CSRs programmatically, retrieving signed certificates, and integrating renewal into pipelines. When using the API, the certificate response is returned as JSON-encoded content and must typically be decoded before use.The SAP BTP Cockpit simplifies the process considerably. The CSR is uploaded directly, the certificate is generated, and the complete chain can be exported in PEM format immediately. No JSON decoding or PEM conversion steps are required.

This blog uses the UI-based approach.

Prerequisites

  • An SAP BTP subaccount with authorization to create service instances
  • An active SAP BTP Destination Service instance (lite plan is sufficient)
  • Administrator access to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Setting Up SAP BTP Destination Service

Create the Destination Service Instance

Navigate to your subaccount in SAP BTP Cockpit, then go to Services > Instances and Subscriptions. If a Destination Service instance does not already exist, click Create and select:

  • Service: Destination
  • Plan: lite
  • Environment: Cloud Foundry (or Other)

Figure 1: Instances and Subscriptions — dest-serv instance in status Created

Once the instance is created, navigate into it and select Destination Certificates from the left navigation. This is where all certificate lifecycle operations are performed.

Figure 2: Service Instance > Destination Certificates — ready to create a new certificate

High-Level Process

For SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, the process follows these steps:

  1. Create a Certificate Signing Request in the Maintain Client Certificates application
  2. Download the CSR file
  3. Upload the CSR to SAP BTP Destination Service and generate the signed certificate
  4. Review the certificate chain
  5. Export the signed certificate chain from BTP Cockpit (PEM format)
  6. Import the certificate response back into S/4HANA Cloud

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Unlike STRUST-based systems, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition does not expose PSE management directly. Certificate management is handled through the Maintain Client Certificates application. When a Certificate Signing Request is created in this application, the private key is generated and stored internally, and the CSR is produced from that key pair. The private key never leaves S/4HANA Cloud.

Step 1: Create a Certificate Signing Request

Navigate to Administration > Security and open the Maintain Client Certificates application.

Figure 3: Maintain Client Certificates — click the Create New Certificate Signing Request icon

Click the Create New Certificate Signing Request icon (top right of the certificate list). A dialog opens. Enable Form-Based Input and provide the following:

  • Description: A meaningful label, for example: S4 Cloud Client Certificate - Signed by SAP BTP Destination Service
  • Name (Common Name): A logical identifier, for example: s4-client-integration-test
  • Public Key Algorithm: RSA
  • Key Strength: 4096
  • Signature Algorithm: SHA256

Figure 4: Certificate Signing Request dialog — form-based input with name, algorithm, and key strength

Click Create Signing Request. S/4HANA Cloud generates the key pair internally and produces the CSR. The certificate entry is created with status CA Response Required.

Figure 5: Generated CSR displayed — ready to download

Step 2: Download the CSR

Open the certificate entry and click Download to save the CSR file locally. Use a .csr extension for clarity, for example: s4-client-integration-test.csr.

Figure 6: CSR displayed with Download button — copy or save the file

Figure 7: Save As dialog — saving as s4-client-integration-test.csr

Step 3: Upload CSR and Sign in SAP BTP Cockpit

Return to SAP BTP Cockpit. Navigate to your Destination Service instance and open Destination Certificates. Click Create.

Figure 8: Destination Certificates page — click Create to issue a new certificate

In the Create Certificate panel, provide the following:

  • Name: A logical name for the certificate, for example: s4-client-integration-test
  • Generation Service: SAP Certificate Service (selected automatically)
  • File Extension: PEM
  • Common Name (CN): Use the same CN as in the CSR, for example: s4-client-integration-test
  • Validity: Choose an appropriate period (for example: 6 months)
  • Automatic Renewal: On (recommended)
  • Certificate Signing Request: Upload the .csr file downloaded from S/4HANA

Figure 9: Create Certificate form — CSR uploaded and details completed

Note: The subject pattern in the uploaded CSR will be overridden by the Destination Service subject pattern. Only the public key from the CSR is used. The private key remains in S/4HANA Cloud.

Figure 10: CSR field tooltip — BTP stores only the public certificate, not the private key

Click Create. SAP BTP signs the CSR and creates the certificate entry.

Step 4: Review the Certificate Chain

Certificate Chain Considerations

After the certificate is issued, open the certificate entry and expand the chain to review the trust hierarchy. Depending on the validity period selected, SAP BTP Destination Service may return different certificate chains.

Certificates with validity greater than one month typically use the full SAP BTP Client CA hierarchy:

  • Client Certificate
  • SAP Cloud Platform Client CA
  • SAP Cloud Root CA

Figure 11: Certificate chain — longer validity, 3-level hierarchy

Certificates with shorter validity periods (one month or less) may include additional intermediate certificates in the chain:

  • Client Certificate
  • SAP PKI Certificate Service Client CA
  • SAP BTP Client CA
  • SAP Cloud Root CA

Figure 12: Certificate chain — shorter validity, 4-level hierarchy with additional intermediate CA

Note: Always export the complete certificate bundle returned by SAP BTP — do not export individual certificates from the chain. The exact chain structure may vary over time as SAP updates certificate profiles.

Step 5: Export the Signed Certificate

Open the certificate entry in BTP Cockpit and click Export. The complete certificate chain is downloaded in PEM format — no further conversion is required.

Figure 13: Export button — downloads the complete PEM certificate chain

Step 6: Import the Certificate Response into S/4HANA Cloud

Return to the Maintain Client Certificates application in SAP S/4HANA Cloud. Locate the certificate entry created in Step 1 (status: CA Response Required). Use the Actions menu and select Import Certificate Response.

Figure 14: Import Certificate Response — selected from the Actions menu

Paste or upload the exported PEM file content into the Certificate Signing Response field and click Import.

Figure 15: Import Certificate Signing Response dialog — paste the PEM content

After successful import, the certificate status changes from CA Response Required to valid. The temporary self-signed certificate is replaced by the SAP BTP-signed chain. The certificate can now be assigned to Communication Systems and used for outbound mTLS scenarios.

Figure 16: Certificate detail after import — valid, signed by SAP Cloud Platform Client CA

No PKCS#12 Conversion Required

When the CSR is generated directly inside SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, there is no need to create a .p12 file or handle private keys manually. The Import Certificate Response action in the Maintain Client Certificates application handles all key association internally.

Summary

SAP BTP Destination Service provides a straightforward, UI-based way to obtain client certificates trusted within the SAP ecosystem — without exposing private key material to any external system.

Key takeaways:

  • Certificates are issued through the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy and are natively trusted across SAP services
  • The private key is generated and retained entirely within SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
  • No PKCS#12 bundling, no JSON decoding, and no PEM conversion is required for the UI-based flow
  • Certificate validity affects the trust chain depth — always export and import the full chain
  • Automatic renewal is available; a re-import is required after each renewal
  • The same capability is also available through the Destination Service REST API for automated lifecycle management

References:

  • SAP Help: Manage Certificates issued by SAP Cloud Root CA
  • SAP API Business Hub: Destination Service

See Also: For SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise deployments using STRUST, refer to the companion blog: "Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud".

entry.title: Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud
entry.content:
Introduction

Many SAP integrations require mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication to securely establish trust between systems. Common scenarios include:

  • SAP S/4HANA outbound integrations
  • Communication arrangements
  • SAP Integration Suite scenarios
  • Partner and third-party API integrations
  • B2B communication channels

To support these scenarios, SAP BTP Destination Service provides a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) capability that can issue client certificates signed by the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy. These certificates are trusted across SAP services and can be used to authenticate outbound calls from SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise systems.

This blog walks through the end-to-end UI-based process for SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise deployments using transaction STRUST: generating a Certificate Signing Request, submitting it to SAP BTP Destination Service, and importing the signed certificate response back into STRUST.

For SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, refer to the companion blog: "Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition".

 

Understanding SAP BTP Destination Service PKI

SAP BTP Destination Service can act as a Certificate Authority service for SAP workloads. It signs Certificate Signing Requests using the SAP Cloud Root CA trust chain, producing certificates that are natively trusted across the SAP ecosystem.

The typical flow is:

  1. Select or create an SSL Client PSE in STRUST
  2. Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) from the PSE
  3. Upload the CSR to SAP BTP Destination Service
  4. SAP BTP signs the CSR using the SAP Cloud Root CA trust chain
  5. Export the signed certificate chain from BTP Cockpit
  6. Import the signed certificate response back into STRUST

Note: The private key never leaves STRUST. SAP BTP only receives the CSR and returns a signed certificate chain.

 

API vs UI Approaches

SAP BTP Destination Service supports both API-based and UI-based certificate issuance.

API-Based

UI-Based

The API approach enables automated certificate lifecycle management: submitting CSRs programmatically, retrieving signed certificates, and integrating renewal into pipelines. When using the API, the certificate response is returned as JSON-encoded content and must typically be decoded before use.The SAP BTP Cockpit simplifies the process considerably. The CSR is uploaded directly, the certificate is generated, and the complete chain can be exported in PEM format immediately. No JSON decoding or PEM conversion steps are required.

This blog uses the UI-based approach.

Prerequisites

  • An SAP BTP subaccount with authorization to create service instances
  • An active SAP BTP Destination Service instance (lite plan is sufficient)
  • Administrator access to SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud or on-premise system
  • Access to transaction STRUST in the target system

Setting Up SAP BTP Destination Service

Create the Destination Service Instance

Navigate to your subaccount in SAP BTP Cockpit, then go to Services > Instances and Subscriptions. If a Destination Service instance does not already exist, click Create and select:

  • Service: Destination
  • Plan: lite
  • Environment: Cloud Foundry (or Other)

 

Figure 1: Instances and Subscriptions — dest-serv instance in status Created

Once the instance is created, navigate into it and select Destination Certificates from the left navigation. This is where all certificate lifecycle operations are performed.

Figure 2: Service Instance > Destination Certificates — ready to create a new certificate

High-Level Process

For SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise systems, the process follows these steps:

  1. Select or create an SSL Client PSE in STRUST
  2. Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) from the PSE
  3. Download the CSR file
  4. Upload the CSR to SAP BTP Destination Service and generate the signed certificate
  5. Export the signed certificate chain from BTP Cockpit (PEM format)
  6. Import the certificate response back into STRUST
  7. Save the PSE

SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud / On-Premise (STRUST)

SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and on-premise systems use transaction STRUST (Trust Manager) to manage PKI and SSL identities. STRUST stores key pairs in Personal Security Environments (PSEs). The process below creates or reuses an SSL Client PSE, generates the CSR from STRUST, gets it signed via SAP BTP, and imports the signed response — all without the private key leaving STRUST.

Step 1: Select or Create an SSL Client PSE

Open transaction STRUST. In the PSE tree on the left, navigate to the SSL Client Identities of System node (Environment > SSL Client Identities of System). Either select an existing SSL Client PSE or create a new one by double-clicking an empty entry and providing an Identity name and Description.

Figure 3: STRUST — SSL Client PSE selected, showing existing certificate and issuer chain

Note: If you are creating a new PSE for this purpose, provide a meaningful identity name and description so the purpose of the certificate is clear to other administrators.

Step 2: Generate the Certificate Signing Request

With the SSL Client PSE selected, choose PSE > Create Certificate Request from the menu bar. An Attributes for Certificate Requests dialog appears. Set the Signature Algorithm to SHA256 and confirm.

Figure 4: STRUST Attributes for Certificate Requests — set Signature Algorithm to SHA256

STRUST generates the CSR from the PSE's existing key pair and displays the certificate request content in a Certificate Request dialog.

Figure 5: STRUST Certificate Request dialog — CSR generated and displayed

Note: The private key used to sign the CSR remains securely in STRUST. Only the CSR, which contains the public key and subject information, is shared externally.

Step 3: Download the CSR File

In the Certificate Request dialog, click the Save to File button (or copy the PEM content). Save the file with a .csr extension, for example: S4-Private-Cloud.csr.

Figure 6: Save As dialog — saving the CSR as S4-Private-Cloud.csr

Step 4: Upload CSR and Sign in SAP BTP Cockpit

Return to SAP BTP Cockpit. Navigate to your Destination Service instance and open Destination Certificates. Click Create.

In the Create Certificate panel, provide the following:

  • Name: A logical name for the certificate, for example: s4-client-destpoc
  • Generation Service: SAP Certificate Service (selected automatically)
  • File Extension: PEM
  • Common Name (CN): A meaningful identifier, for example: s4-client-destpoc
  • Validity: Choose an appropriate period (for example: 1 year)
  • Automatic Renewal: On (recommended)
  • Certificate Signing Request: Upload the .csr file downloaded from STRUST

Figure 7: Create Certificate form in BTP Cockpit — CSR uploaded with Private Cloud details

Click Create. SAP BTP signs the CSR and creates the certificate entry.

Note: The subject pattern in the uploaded CSR will be overridden by the Destination Service subject pattern. Only the public key from the CSR is used. The private key remains in STRUST.

Step 5: Export the Signed Certificate

Open the new certificate entry in BTP Cockpit and review the certificate chain. The chain should show the client certificate signed by the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy. Click Export to download the complete certificate chain in PEM format.

Figure 8: Certificate detail expanded — validity dates, subject, and issuer hierarchy

Figure 9: Signed certificate detail — trust chain visible, Export button highlighted 

Note: Always export the complete certificate bundle, not individual entries from the chain. The exact chain structure may vary over time as SAP updates certificate profiles.

Step 6: Import the Certificate Response into STRUST

Return to transaction STRUST. Select the same SSL Client PSE used to generate the CSR. Choose PSE > Import Certificate Response (or use the Certificate menu). Paste the PEM content from the exported file into the Certificate Response dialog and confirm.

Figure 10: STRUST Certificate Response dialog — paste the PEM content from BTP Export

After importing, STRUST matches the signed certificate to the existing private key in the PSE and displays the updated certificate details. The Own Certificate field now shows the new subject issued by the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy.

Figure 11: STRUST after certificate response import — new issuer chain visible

Save the PSE

Click Save (or PSE > Save As to save to a named PSE file) to persist the changes. The signed certificate is now active and the PSE is ready for use in outbound mTLS scenarios.

Figure 12: STRUST certificate details — validity, subject, issuer, algorithm confirmed

Summary

SAP BTP Destination Service provides a straightforward, UI-based way to obtain client certificates trusted within the SAP ecosystem — without exposing private key material to any external system.

Key takeaways:

  • Certificates are issued through the SAP Cloud Root CA hierarchy and are natively trusted across SAP services
  • The private key is generated and retained entirely within STRUST — only the CSR is shared with SAP BTP
  • No PKCS#12 bundling, no JSON decoding, and no PEM conversion is required for the UI-based flow
  • Certificate validity affects the trust chain depth — always export and import the full chain
  • STRUST's Import Certificate Response action matches the signed certificate to the existing private key automatically
  • Automatic renewal is available in BTP; a re-import into STRUST is required after each renewal
  • The same capability is also available through the Destination Service REST API for automated lifecycle management

Reference:

  • SAP Help: Manage Certificates issued by SAP Cloud Root CA
  • SAP API Business Hub: Destination Service

See Also: For SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition deployments using the Maintain Client Certificates application, refer to the companion blog: "Issuing Client Certificates via SAP BTP Destination Service for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition".

entry.title: Step-by-Step Setup of OAuth2 SAML2 Bearer with Principal Propagation with on-prem ABAP with BTP CPI
entry.content:
As security requirements continue to grow, many SAP integrations are moving away from traditional Basic Authentication and shifting to stronger approaches such as OAuth 2.0, Mutual TLS (mTLS), and Principal Propagation. These mechanisms help protect communication between on-premises SAP systems and SAP BTP services while also improving trust, traceability, and identity-based access control. Even though the overall setup may look simple in an architecture diagram, building the full end-to-end flow can be complex because several components must be configured correctly and must work together.

In this implementation, the goal was to build a secure connection between an on-premises SAP ABAP system and SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) on SAP BTP without depending on technical users or stored passwords. Instead, the solution uses OAuth-based authentication, certificate trust through mTLS, and Principal Propagation so that the original business user identity can be passed securely across the entire integration flow. To make this work, trust had to be configured carefully across SAP ABAP, CPI, SAP Cloud Connector, and the target backend system.

SAP provides documentation for many of these individual areas, but it is often difficult to find one complete guide that explains the full authentication and identity propagation journey from start to finish. This blog is intended to close that gap by presenting the architecture, the configuration approach, and the main lessons learned during the implementation.

Although this setup was implemented in SAP BTP Neo Cloud Integration, the same overall concept can also be applied to Cloud Foundry and to other SAP BTP services that require secure communication between cloud and on-premises SAP systems.

 

Architecture Overview

The runtime flow begins in the SAP ABAP system, where the consumer proxy initiates the outbound request using OAuth 2.0 with a SAML 2.0 Bearer assertion. CPI on SAP BTP acts as the receiving side, while the trust configuration and Principal Propagation setup ensure that the originating user identity is preserved across the communication path. As a result, CPI can process the inbound trusted request securely, allowing the end-to-end integration to function without the need for a static technical password.

 

 

Prerequisites

  • A BTP/CPI subaccount with access to build trust configuration and user authorization.
  • An ABAP backend with access to build OAuth 2.0 profile creation and SOAMANAGER.
  • Cloud Connector accesses the connect BTP subaccount and set-up principal propagation.
  • mTLS trust already established between Cloud connector with ABAP with/without Web-dispatcher in-between.

Step 1. Create the OAuth Client in CPI

The first step is to create the OAuth client configuration in CPI that supports the inbound integration flow originating from the SAP ABAP system. This configuration is required so CPI can receive and process requests secured through OAuth 2.0 with a SAML 2.0 Bearer assertion.

CPI Subaccount -> Security -> OAuth

In the client details, create the OAuth client using the "Client Credentials" option. Generate the "Client ID" and "Client Secret" and store them safely, as they will be required later to establish trust with the back-end ABAP system. For iFlow-based communication, choose the subscription for "iflmap".

Other details about the authorization server, such as the "Token Service URL" and "Authorization Service URL", are also available in this section. These details are required later when authenticating the incoming request from the SAP ABAP system. ABAP will use these details to get tokens generated.

 

Step 2. Create Local Service Provider Settings

After the client is created, the next step is to create the trust setup and prepare CPI to work with different identity providers. In this step, create a custom service provider, as this is required to integrate the external identity provider as the application identity provider that will be configured later. Also make sure to note the "Local Provider Name (URL)".

CPI Subaccount -> Security -> Trust

 

Step 3. Configure the ABAP OAuth 2.0 Profile

On the ABAP side, create an OAuth profile in the ABAP Workbench. Below is the standard code snippet used for this setup.

 

*Access Oauth2.0 client profile configuration

    TRY.
        CALL METHOD cl_oauth2_client=>create
          EXPORTING
            i_profile        = i_profile
            i_configuration  = i_config
          RECEIVING
            ro_oauth2_client = DATA(lo_oauth2_client).

      CATCH cx_oa2c INTO lo_oa2c.
        es_return = VALUE #( type = lc_e
                          message = |Unbale to Get OAuth 2.0 Client with | &&
                                    |profile: { i_profile } and Config: { i_config }| ).
        RETURN.
    ENDTRY.

*Call the below method to access any generated Token within time frame of the the Token Expiry Time((For example: 15 min)
*This method call will be failed every time when the token is expired.
    TRY.
        CALL METHOD lo_oauth2_client->set_token
          EXPORTING
            io_http_client = lo_http_client
            i_param_kind   = i_param_kind.

      CATCH cx_oa2c INTO lo_oa2c.


*Call the below method to generate the token in every Token Expiry time (For example: 15 min)
*The token will be internall saved in SAP tables/ICF. To enhance the security, the token would not be accessible out in the code.

        TRY.
            CALL METHOD lo_oauth2_client->execute_cc_flow.
          CATCH cx_oa2c INTO lo_oa2c.
            es_return = VALUE #( type = lc_e
                              message = |Unable to Execute Client Credentials Flow| ).
            RETURN.
        ENDTRY.

*Call the below method to access any generated Token within time frame of the the Token Expiry Time((For example: 15 min)
*This method call will be successful when method execute_cc_flow call is successfully executed.

        TRY.
            CALL METHOD lo_oauth2_client->set_token
              EXPORTING
                io_http_client = lo_http_client
                i_param_kind   = i_param_kind.
          CATCH cx_oa2c INTO lo_oa2c.
            es_return = VALUE #( type = lc_e
                              message = |Unable to Set Access Token in HTTP-Client| ).
            RETURN.
        ENDTRY.
    ENDTRY.

 

SAP has provided enhancement/BAdI "OA2C_SPECIFICS" to make adjustments in the standard code and configuration settings. A custom BAdI class has to be implemented using the superclass "CL_OA2C_SPECIFICS_ABSTRACT". The required methods can then be redefined as needed.

Follow the below reference link for more details:

https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/configuring-oauth-2-0-and-creating-an-abap-program-that-uses-oauth-2-0/ba-p/13470572

Once the OAuth profile is created, configure it further in ABAP by maintaining all the required settings and details needed for this integration scenario.

Tcode: SOAUTH2_CLIENT

Client ID: Same ID created in Step 1

Client Secret: Same secret created in Step 1

Token Endpoint: Token endpoint of the CPI authorization server from Step 1

Also make sure SAML2 attributes are activated.

SAML2 Audience URL: The CPI custom service provider URL created in Step 2

SAML2 Recipient: The CPI authorization server token URL from Step 1

SAML2 User Mapping Mechanism: Choose email

Once done, make sure you download the SAML2 metadata for ABAP. This will be needed to onboard your ABAP system into CPI.

 

Step 4. on board your ABAP SAML2 details into CPI

In the next step, create the "Application Identity Provider" for ABAP in CPI. In the previous step, ABAP was configured to recognize CPI as the authorization server, and now CPI must be configured to trust ABAP by establishing the trust relationship between the two systems. Once the "Application Identity Provider" is created in CPI, the system is able to accept and process the SAML 2.0 Bearer assertions issued by the ABAP system during the OAuth flow.

In CPI, add ABAP as your identity provider by clicking "Add Trusted Identity Provider" and uploading the SAML2 metadata downloaded from ABAP.

CPI Subaccount -> Trust -> Application Identity Provider

Make sure to verify the below details.

Single Sign-On URL: You can use your ABAP FQDN as the URL

Single Logout URL: Same as above



 

Step 5. Map Assertion Attributes and Backend Groups

Once ABAP is established as the identity provider in CPI, make sure the required attributes are created there as well. This ensures that any ABAP attributes carried by the ABAP system while initiating the call can be matched correctly with the CPI configuration.

Proper attribute maintenance is important so that the attributes sent by ABAP are recognized and mapped accordingly during the authentication process. This allows the user information and context received from ABAP to be processed seamlessly throughout the authentication flow.

Click on the newly created ABAP identity provider to edit it. In the same ABAP identity provider, maintain the attributes and group settings as shown below.

Next, create an authorization group in CPI for the user and assign the required permissions so the users assigned to it can perform the necessary activities within CPI. In this step, create a new group with any suitable name, such as "Oauth2_user", and assign the permissions as shown below.

Once the group is created, the same ABAP calling user needs to be assigned to this group in CPI. This ensures that the user initiating the call from the ABAP system inherits the required permissions and authorizations available through the group within CPI.

CPI Subaccount -> Security -> Authorization -> Groups

Next, make sure the ABAP identity provider uses this group as the default group for authorization, and also create a mapping rule. Ideally, use a wildcard pattern that matches your company domain, such as ".*@yourcompany.com$".

Again, go back to the ABAP identity provider and open it.

CPI Subaccount -> Security -> Trust -> Application Identity Provider

Step 6. Create the Destination with OAuth2 SAML2 Bearer

Finally, create a destination in CPI. Once the Principal Propagation setting is configured in the CPI sender configuration, this destination is used through the SAP Connectivity service to retrieve and propagate the required user attributes for the outbound call.

CPI Subaccount -> Connectivity -> Destination

URL: Only your provider company FQDN; do not add any path to it. CPI iFlows will use the rest of the URL from the sender channel definition.

Proxy: Internet

Authentication: OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion

Audience: The URL of your CPI service provider created in Step 2

AuthnContextClassRef: urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509

Token Service URL: Same token URL from your CPI OAuth client in Step 1

Client Key: Client ID from Step 1

Token Service User: Client ID again from Step 1

Token Service Password: Client Secret from Step 1

 

Step 7. Configure Principal Propagation in Cloud Connector

Note: The detailed configuration of Principal Propagation using SAP Web Dispatcher as an SSL terminator and reverse proxy is outside the scope of this blog. Since several excellent SAP Community articles already provide step-by-step instructions for that setup, this blog focuses primarily on the OAuth, mTLS, and end-to-end identity propagation aspects of the solution.

For the outbound call, Cloud Connector is responsible for securely forwarding the identity into the on-premises landscape. The mapping between the exposed virtual host and the internal host is combined with Principal Propagation so that the backend call remains identity-aware beyond the network boundary.

As a first step, onboard your CPI subaccount to Cloud Connector. Once it is onboarded, make sure to sync the trust between CPI as the service provider and your ABAP system as the identity provider.

Cloud Connector -> Open your CPI subaccount -> Cloud To On-Premises -> Principal Propagation

The next step is to create a mapping with Type "X509 certificate".

Open Cloud Connector -> Select your subaccount -> Cloud To On-Premise -> Access Control

Virtual Host: You can choose any logical name for your backend ABAP

Virtual Port: Any port number for your backend ABAP

Internal Host: Your actual ABAP host or FQDN

Internal Port: Your actual ABAP HTTPS port. Remember, for Principal Propagation it has to be HTTPS. If your ABAP system does not have an active HTTPS port, please set that up first.

This mapping is the operational gateway between cloud runtime and the on-premises backend. When Principal Propagation is enabled correctly, Cloud Connector does not just forward traffic; it forwards trusted identity context together with the request path.

The next step is to create a sample certificate that will be used for mapping in the ABAP system. Make sure the sample certificate contains the correct attributes so that the forwarded X.509 Common Name (CN) matches the certificate mapping maintained in ABAP. This is important to ensure that the propagated user identity is recognized correctly and the appropriate authorizations are assigned during processing.

Cloud Connector -> Configuration -> On-Premises -> Principal Propagation

You can verify the actual attributes reaching Cloud Connector in the traces.

Cloud Connector -> Select your CPI subaccount -> Logging and Tracing -> SCC_Core

Make sure to turn on trace level to Debug and CPIC level to 2.

I used the below attributes for mapping in ABAP.

In ABAP:

Tcode: CERTRULE

Also make sure the calling user in ABAP has email mapping in SU01.

 

Step 8. Activate OAuth 2.0 in the ABAP Consumer Proxy

At the consumer proxy level, the service call is instructed to use OAuth 2.0 rather than Basic Authentication or certificate-only patterns. This aligns the application-layer service consumer with the identity model that was prepared in the previous steps.

SOAMANAGER -> Web Service Configuration

In the below example, I am using the standard proxy: CO_ECPAOX_EE_MD_ORGAS_BNDL_QRY

In the authorization setting, use the OAuth profile created in Step 3.

This setting is important because backend trust alone is not enough. The consuming service object itself must be configured to execute the call using the OAuth profile that matches the propagated identity scenario.

Step 9. Validate End-to-End Connectivity

Validation should prove both connectivity and identity-aware execution. A successful ping confirms technical reachability, while message monitoring confirms that the business-facing integration scenario completed successfully.

The ping result is the initial proof that the destination and connectivity chain are working. It does not replace full functional validation, but it quickly confirms that the path and trust configuration are at least technically usable.

Next, once you activate Principal Propagation in the CPI sender channels, the end-to-end flow is complete. You can verify the successful propagation of user attributes from AS ABAP through CPI and back to ABAP.

The final runtime view should show a completed message or successful processing indicator. This demonstrates that the OAuth client, trust configuration, Principal Propagation, and backend execution have all aligned correctly in one full transaction.

This setup shows how SAP ABAP, CPI, and Cloud Connector can work together to build a secure and identity-aware integration using OAuth 2.0, SAML 2.0 Bearer assertions, and Principal Propagation. Instead of relying on stored technical credentials, the solution allows the original user identity to be trusted, carried forward, and used throughout the complete integration flow. In this example, the setup uses the identity of the calling ABAP user, especially the email address stored in the ABAP user master record, and carries that user context through the entire flow until it reaches the target ABAP system again.

Although the overall process involves several configuration steps across CPI, ABAP, Cloud Connector, trust settings, destinations, and authorization mapping, each step plays an important role in making the end-to-end scenario work correctly. Once all components are aligned properly, the result is a more secure, auditable, and controlled integration pattern for communication between on-premises SAP systems and SAP BTP services.

entry.title: Identity and Access Management with Microsoft Entra, Part IV: Integration with SAP Cloud IAG
entry.content:
This scenario extends the architecture introduced in part III by shifting responsibility for provisioning SAP role assignments from SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS), Identity Provisioning, to SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG). Microsoft Entra ID Governance manages the access package and its assignment lifecycle, while SAP IAG applies SAP-specific approval workflows, risk controls, and downstream role provisioning. The scenario introduces the new SAP IAG connector in Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Azure Key Vault for securely storing the credential when calling the SAP IAG REST API.

 

Note 📢

Interested in connecting with us and discuss your SAP and Entra scenario? Then join the SAP and Microsoft identity teams at SAP TechEd 2026 in Berlin, and add hands-on session XP263 to your event agenda, where you will learn how SAP Cloud Identity Services, SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance, and Microsoft Entra work together to unify user lifecycle management and governance across SAP and third-party application.

Scenario Overview

The architecture for part IV builds on the identity provisioning scenario introduced in part III of this blog series. Microsoft Entra ID remains the central service ("source of authority", SOA) for identity data, and SAP CIS continues to receive users from Microsoft Entra and provisions them to downstream SAP target systems, such as the SAP system on-premises in the corporate network shown in figure 1.
Figure 1: Scenario Overview

 

However, responsibility for provisioning application access to the SAP backend system changes. In part III, SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Provisioning created the backend roles as groups in Microsoft Entra configured as a target system, and translated group memberships provisioned with the Entra SCIM-based SAP CIS provisioning connector into role assignments in the SAP backend system.

In this new scenario, SAP IAG takes over responsibility for governing and provisioning the user’s role assignment to the SAP backend system. Instead of directly translating a Microsoft Entra group assignment into an SAP role assignment, Microsoft Entra now requests access to an SAP IAG business role. SAP IAG processes the access request, applies the configured approval workflow and access controls, and provisions the underlying technical role to the target SAP backend system.
This separation allows each platform to focus on its core capabilities:
  • Microsoft Entra ID Governance provides the entitlement catalogs, access packages, request policies, and the user-facing Microsoft My Access portal.
  • SAP IAG provides SAP business roles, SAP-specific access request workflows, access analysis, risk evaluation, mitigation controls, and provisioning to connected SAP applications in the Cloud and on-premises.
  • SAP CIS maintains the shared user identities and supports identity synchronization between Microsoft Entra and SAP IAG.
  • SAP BTP connectivity service and SAP Cloud Connector provide the technical connection from SAP IAG to the SAP backend system on-premises.
From all components and configurations marked as "new" in figure 1, the SAP IAG tenant is the most important addition to the architecture in this scenario. SAP IAG maintains the business roles that can be requested through Microsoft Entra and maps those business roles to technical roles in connected SAP applications.
In the example scenario, the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the SAP ABAP system A4H. This business role is included in a new Microsoft Entra access package SAP EPM IAG and requested by the user Linda Larson. Microsoft Entra does not provision the underlying ABAP role directly. Instead, Microsoft Entra creates an access request in SAP IAG by calling the SAP IAG Access Request Service API. SAP IAG processes the request and, after the configured workflow has completed successfully, provisions the technical role to the target system.
SAP CIS Identity Provisioning remains part of the wider landscape, particularly when SAP IAG connects to supported cloud applications through Identity Provisioning proxy systems. However, SAP IAG now governs the access decision and orchestrates the provisioning operation for the requested SAP business role.
For this integration, Microsoft Entra ID Governance introduces an SAP IAG connector. The connector establishes the integration between Microsoft Entra entitlement management and the SAP IAG tenant. The connector enables administrators to:
  • Add an SAP IAG tenant as a resource to a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog
  • Discover SAP IAG business roles
  • Add SAP IAG business roles to Microsoft Entra access packages
  • Create SAP IAG access requests when an access package is assigned
  • Initiate removal requests when an assignment expires or is revoked
  • Retrieve the processing status of SAP IAG access requests
All of the actions above will be executed in the exercises of this blog series scenario. The connector communicates with SAP IAG through the Access Request Service REST APIs and authenticates by using OAuth 2.0 client credentials which require a secure storage option offered by the Azure Key Vault service to store the SAP IAG API OAuth client secret used by the SAP IAG connector. When configuring the connector in Microsoft Entra, the administrator selects the Azure subscription, Key Vault, and secret. The SAP IAG client ID, OAuth token URL, and SAP IAG API URL are configured as additional connector properties coming from the service key created for the SAP IAG API service instance in the SAP BTP subaccount.
 
SAP CIS remains essential to this scenario. Microsoft Entra provisions users to the Identity Directory in the SAP CIS tenant through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, RFC 7644). These users and their identifiers are subsequently synchronized into the SAP IAG repository. The Microsoft Entra user's globally unique object ID is mapped to the SAP Global User ID to provide a stable identity correlation across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG. Manager information must also be synchronized when SAP IAG workflows use the user’s manager as an approver. The scenario therefore governs role access for existing users who must already exist in SAP CIS and in the SAP IAG repository before Microsoft Entra submits the SAP IAG access request.
The target SAP applications must be registered and connected to SAP IAG. The provisioning mechanism depends on the application type:
  • For an on-premises system like the SAP Application Server ABAP, SAP IAG uses an SAP BTP destination, the SAP Connectivity service, SAP Cloud Connector, and the required BAPI or RFC interfaces.
  • For supported cloud applications, SAP IAG can use SAP Identity Provisioning proxy systems and the IPS_PROXY destination configured in the BTP subaccount.
The five steps shown in the scenario diagram of figure 1 illustrate the complete access governance process:
  1. Microsoft Entra provisions the users required in SAP IAG (Linda Larson, Tina Johnson & your Entra administrator user) and their SAP IAG roles as group memberships to SAP CIS through the existing enterprise application and SCIM provisioning connection (Note: inbound- or HR-driven provisioning of the test users in this scenario from SAP SuccessFactors to the corporate Active Directory and from there to Entra does not change from the scenario in part III of this blog series). The provisioning configuration must synchronize the Microsoft Entra object ID of the users as the SAP Global User ID. Manager information must also be synchronized if the SAP IAG workflow uses manager-based approval. In this scenario, Tina Johnson is assigned in Active Directory as the manager of Linda Larson and can approve Linda's access request in SAP IAG. After provisioning from Entra to SAP CIS is complete, the relevant SAP IAG synchronization jobs must import the user, groups, and identifiers from SAP CIS into SAP IAG's user repository. All users must be available in SAP IAG before an access request can be submitted from Microsoft Entra.
  2. Linda Larson opens the Microsoft My Access portal and requests the SAP EPM IAG access package. The access package is maintained in a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog and contains the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM.
  3. The SAP IAG connector calls the SAP IAG APIs and creates an access request for the user and selected business role. SAP IAG validates the request and that the user exists in its repository.
  4. SAP IAG processes the request according to the workflow and governance configuration of the SAP IAG tenant. Depending on the organization’s configuration, processing can include manager approval, segregation of duties (SOD) analysis, critical access analysis, assignment of mitigation controls and other steps. In this scenario, Tina Johnson as the manager of Linda Larson needs to approve Linda's access request. Microsoft Entra governs eligibility for the access package and its assignment lifecycle. SAP IAG governs the SAP-specific role assignment and applies SAP-specific risk and compliance controls.
  5. After the SAP IAG workflow has completed successfully, SAP IAG provisions the business role to the connected target applications. In the scenario, the business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the ABAP system A4H. SAP IAG uses the configured SAP BTP destination to reach the target system through SAP Cloud Connector and invokes the required BAPIs. The result is the assignment of SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO to Linda Larson's user in the SAP backend system.

For a live demo, check out episode #307 of the SAP on Azure video podcast, where @Holger-Bruchelt and I go through the scenario step by step.

Microsoft Entra continues to manage the lifecycle of the access package assignment. If the assignment expires or is revoked, Microsoft Entra uses the SAP IAG connector to initiate a removal request. SAP IAG processes that request and deprovisions the corresponding role from the target system. As part of the following exercises, the Microsoft Entra tenant administrator removes Linda's assignment to the SAP EPM IAG access package to test deprovisioning in the scenario.

Prerequisites

Note 📢

This tutorial extends and updates the scenario from part I, part II, and part III. If you arrived here without having completed these three parts of the tutorial series, please do so first, and then come back again.

 
The following additional components and configurations are required to implement SAP IAG-based access governance and role provisioning:
  • An entitlement for the SAP IAG test or standard application plan, and an application subscription to your SAP IAG tenant in the BTP subaccount that is already subscribed to your SAP CIS connectivity plan (see part II) and trusts the SAP CIS tenant as the application identity provider.
  • Administrative access to the SAP IAG tenant with a user assigned to SAP IAG's CIAG_Super_Admin role collection to configure the required settings for this scenario.
  • An entitlement for the SAP IAG standard service plan (technical service name "grc-iag-api"), and a service instance in your BTP subaccount's Cloud Foundry environment to create the service key for accessing your SAP IAG tenant's API with the Entra connector. This is the first step of the following exercises to build the scenario.
  • An Azure subscription with a trust relationship to the Microsoft Entra tenant, and at least administrative access with a user assigned to the Contributor role on a resource group to create the Azure Key Vault instance. The Key Vault stores the SAP IAG API client secret from the service key used by Microsoft Entra to obtain an OAuth access token from SAP BTP to call the SAP IAG API.
  • A new test user Tina Johnson (account name tjohnson) created in the Active Directory (AD) and synchronized to the Cloud with  the Entra Provisioning Agent on-premises and Entra Cloud Sync as described in steps 10.5 to 10.12 of part III. Tina Johnson is the approver of the access request in SAP IAG in this scenario. Linda Larson (account name llarson), who was already on-boarded (steps 9 and 10) in part III, will be used as the user requesting access in this scenario. To make tjohnson the approver in this scenario, she must be assigned as the manager of llarson in AD. Note: You can also test the scenario with users created and managed directly in Entra ID and that do not originate from the on-premises AD. In this case, also make sure that user tjohnson is set as the manager in user llarson's job information profile settings.

Create the SAP IAG API service key

We get started with generating the credentials that are required to authorize the SAP IAG Access Request API calls from the connector in Microsoft Entra.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
1.1

Login to SAP BTP Cockpit and select your subaccount. Navigate to Services → Instances and Subscriptions.
In the list of your subaccount's service instances, click on the ellipsis (•••) of the SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance service instance for the standard plan.

Click Create Service Key from the menu.

1.2

Enter a name for the new service key.

Click Create.

1.3Wait for the completion of the service key operation. Then select it from the list.
1.4

Switch to the Form tab.

Copy and paste the following service key properties to a temporary file:

  • ARQAPI
  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url
You will need these values for the configuration of the connector in Entra.
Click Close.

Create the Azure Key Vault

The SAP IAG connector in Entra requires the service key credentials (client id and client secret) to obtain an access token from the SAP BTP Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA) service to call the SAP IAG tenant's APIs. The connector uses Azure Key Vault to reduces the risk of accidental leaks and ensures that sensitive information like the client secret is stored securely. 

If you already have an Azure Key Vault instance created in your subscription, you can use it in this scenario and jump to step 2.6. Otherwise continue with step 2.1.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
2.1

Login with your Azure administrator account to the Azure Portal.

Click Create a Resource.

2.2

Enter "Key Vault" in the search bar and hit Enter.

On the Key Vault tile in the search results, click Create.

2.3

Select an existing Resource Group or click Create new to create a new one.

Provide a Name (for example "sapiagkv"), select a Region (for example "East US"), and select "Standard" for the Pricing tier.

Keep the other default settings and click Review + create.

2.4Review the Key Vault configuration and click Create.
2.5When the deployment of the new Key Vault is complete, click Go to resource.
2.6

Navigate to Objects → Secrets.

Click Generate/Import.

2.7

Provide a name for new secret (for example "SAPIAGAPIKey"), and copy/paste the value of  clientsecret from step 1.4 into the Secret value field. Make sure you don't have any whitespace characters at the beginning or end of the copied string.

Click Create.

Configure required user attribute mappings

To have a common and globally unique user identifier in this scenario across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG, the user's object id in Entra will be used to fill the following SAP CIS SCIM user attributes:

  • userName
  • externalId
  • urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:sap:2.0:User:userUuid

The last attribute from the list above defines the user's SAP Global User ID which uniquely identifies the user across SAP business applications and services. By filling it with the objectId from the user in Entra we are following the alternative approach as described here and do not rely on SAP CIS to generate the ID in this scenario.

The following step assume that you already have created the enterprise application for the SAP CIS tenant in Microsoft Entra as described in steps 6.1 to 6.23 from part II.

 
StepDescriptionScreenshot
3.1

Login to the Microsoft Entra admin center with your Entra administrator user.

Navigate to Entra ID → Enterprise Applications and select the enterprise application for your SAP CIS tenant from the list.

Select Provisioning from the enterprise application menu.

3.2

Select Attribute mapping from the menu.

On the Users tab, search for the userName target attribute in the list and click the pencil (edit) symbol.

3.3

In the Source attribute (Microsoft Entra ID) drop-down list, select objectId.

Click Apply.

3.4

Repeat steps 3.2 and 3.3 with the following SAP CIS target attributes:

  • externalId
  • urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:sap:2.0:User:userUuid
3.5Verify that the target attribute urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:enterprise:2.0:User:manager is mapped to the manager source attribute from Microsoft Entra ID.

Create SAP IAG user groups and assign test users

SAP IAG requires a set of specific groups that it looks for when users access the service for administration, workflow approvals, or requesting a business role. Instead of creating these required groups in SAP CIS as described in the SAP IAG admin guide, we create them in Entra and provision them to the SAP CIS tenant with the test users assigned to them.

Note 📢

You only create a subset of the required groups needed for the Access Request service. Other SAP IAG services such as Privileged Access Management are out of scope for this scenario.

 

StepDescriptionScreenshot
4.1

Navigate to Entra ID → Groups.

Click New Group.

4.2

For the Group name, enter IAG_RAA_DEFAULT.

Click Create.

Repeat this step for the following groups:

  • IAG_USER
  • IAG_RCA_DEFAULT
  • IAG_WF_MANAGER
  • IAG_SUPER_ADMIN
4.3

Navigate to Entra ID → Users.

Search for user Linda Larson. If you haven't created this test user (see steps 9 and 10 in part III) yet, please onboard it now either in SAP SuccessFactors, as a new user in Active Directory, or directly in Entra.

Note 📢:  Make sure that the user has an e-mail address configured. If you are using an M365 developer tenant, assign the test user an M365 E5 Developer license in your tenant.

Select Groups from the menu and click Add membership.

4.4

Select the group IAG_USER from the list and click Select.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for user Tina Johnson to be the assignment approver in the access request workflow for the business role created in steps 13.x by assigning her the groups IAG_RAA_DEFAULT, IAG_WF_MANAGER and IAG_USER.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for user Alex Carter to be the content approver for the business role created in steps 13.x by assigning him the group IAG_RCA_DEFAULT.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for your Entra administrator user to be the SAP IAG administrator by assigning this user the group IAG_SUPER_ADMIN.

4.5

Navigate back to Entra ID → Users and search again for user Linda Larson.

On the Overview page, select the Properties tab.

Scroll down to the Job Information category. Check if Tina Johnson is assigned as the Manager.

If not, either set Tina Johnson as the manager directly in the Entra admin center (if they are cloud-only user accounts), or set her as the manager in the Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) tool (for on-premises AD user accounts).

Provision SAP IAG groups and users to SAP CIS and SAP ABAP system

The new SAP IAG groups and their assignments to the test users are provisioned to the SAP CIS tenant, and from the tenan's Local Directory with the existing configuration from part II, steps 9.x, in the Identity Provisioning Service (IPS) to the downstream SAP ABAP system A4H.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
5.1

In the Entra admin center, go back to Entra ID → Enterprise Applications and select the enterprise application for your SAP CIS tenant from the list. Select Provisioning from the enterprise application menu.

Select Users and Groups from the provisioning menu, and click Add user/group.

5.2Select None selected.
5.3

Search for "IAG_" and select all groups created in step 4.2 from the search results.

Click Select.

5.4Click Assign.
5.5

Select Provision on demand from the menu.

Search for IAG_RAA_DEFAULT in the Select a user or group field.

Select the group from the search results.

5.6

Select View members only.

From the drop-down list, select Tina Johnson.

Click Provision.

5.7

In the Perform action report you can see that the group and user has been created in the SAP CIS tenant and that the user has been assigned as a member.

Close the report.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_WF_MANAGER and user Tina Johnson.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_USER and users Linda Larson and Tina Johnson.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_RCA_DEFAULT and user Alex Carter.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_SUPER_ADMIN and your Entra administrator user.

5.8

Login as the administrator to your SAP CIS tenant.

Navigate to Identity Provisioning → Source Systems.

5.9

Select the LocalDirectory source system configured in part II, step 9.4, from the list.

Switch to the Jobs tab.

For the Read Job Type, click Run Now.

5.10

Verify the success provisioning of the new users from the SAP CIS tenant's Local Directory to the SAP ABAP system A4H.

Navigate to Identity Provisioning → Provisioning Logs.

511

Select the most recent job from the list.

From the job Statistics, verify that the user row for the system SAPA4H shows the number users created in SAP ABAP backend system.

Configure Attributes in SAP CIS

Instead of directly assigning the SAP IAG users to the pre-delivered role collections in SAP IAG, we map the previously provisioned SAP IAG groups and memberships in SAP CIS to these role collections. Therefore a new "Groups" attribute must be added to the security token (assertion) issued by SAP CIS to SAP IAG. In addition, the user's first name. last name, and email address with the attribute names defined in the SAP IAG admin guide need to be added.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
6.1

Navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications.

6.2

From the Bundled Applications list, select your SAP BTP subaccount containing the SAP IAG subscription.

Note: If your SAP IAG tenant is listed as a subelement of the SAP BTP subaccount, then select this entry.

Under Trust settings, click on Attributes.

6.3Click Add.
6.4

For the new attribute enter the following values:

  • Name: Groups (with uppercase 'G')
  • Source: Identity Directory
  • Value: All Groups

Repeat steps 6.3 and 6.4 for the following additional attributes required by SAP IAG (Source is always Identity Directory)

  • Name: first_name, Value: First Name
  • Name: last_name, Value: Last Name
  • Name: mail, Value: Email

Click Save.

Map SAP CIS groups to SAP IAG role collections

With the new attributes added to the SAP CIS issued token, we now can map the SAP IAG role collections required for this scenario to the groups. So whenever a user is assigned to any of these groups in Entra, provisioning with the SAP CIS enterprise app synchronizes these entities to SAP CIS, from where SAP IAG receives the token for the user containing the user's group memberships, and SAP IAG provides the authorization with the matching role collection.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
7.1Sign-on to the SAP BTP Cockpit with your BTP administrator and select your BTP subaccount with your SAP IAG tenant's subscription
7.2

Navigate to Security → Role Collections.

From the list of role collections, select CIAG_Display.

7.3

Switch to the User Groups tab.

Click Edit.

7.4

From the Identity Provider drop-down list, select your SAP CIS tenant.

For the group name, enter IAG_USER.

Click Save.

7.5

Repeat steps 7.2 to 7.4 for role collection CIAG_Super_Admin and user group name IAG_SUPER_ADMIN.

Synchronize SAP CIS Users and Groups with SAP IAG

With all user and group information that applies to SAP IAG administration and access request workflows in this scenario stored in the SAP CIS, this content must be synchronized between SAP CIS and SAP IAG through a job called SCI User Group Sync in the SAP IAG tenant.

Note 📢

This step requires that the initial configuration in the SAP BTP subaccount and SAP IAG tenant for the SCI User Group Sync job is already done. Please refer to the detailed instructions in the SAP IAG admin guide to configure the following prerequisites to run the sync job:

  • Create SAP IAG Sync system and secret as the SAP CIS administrator in your SAP CIS tenant
  • Create and configure the destination SAP_Identity_Services_Identity_Directory as the SAP BTP administrator in your SAP BTP subaccount
  • As the SAP IAG administrator, set the Application Parameter for SourceSystem in Configuration Group UserSource to the value SAP_Identity_Services_Identity_Directory in the Configuration app in SAP IAG.

 

StepDescriptionScreenshot
8.1

Open the URL of your SAP IAG tenant in a new browser tab.

You will be prompted to select the identity provider for logon. Choose your SAP CIS tenant from the list.

8.2

Login as the SAP IAG administrator with your Entra administrator user, who is now assigned to the IAG_SUPER_ADMIN group that maps to the CIAG_Super_Admin role collection, to your SAP IAG tenant.

With the Entra tenant being configured as the corporate Identity Provider (see step 1.x and 2.x in part I) in your SAP CIS tenant, login to SAP IAG is delegated to the Entra tenant. 

8.3

From the SAP IAG launchpad, click Job Scheduler.

8.4

Enter a name for the new job and choose Job Category SCI User Group Sync Job.

Click Schedule Job.
