entry.title: SAP BTP Work Zone - Authentication and Authorization, with On prem system
entry.content:
Recently I was working on deploying apps from SAP BTP and an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system to SAP Build Work Zone. The most important question from stakeholders was: how does access actually work when the app itself lives in S/4HANA? This post answers that question first with a simple example, and then walks through the configuration I used to make it work.

To make it easy to understand, imagine you run an enterprise called Central Inc. You want every employee to have one single launchpad to access apps from different systems: S/4HANA (Finance), SuccessFactors (HR) and Ariba (Procurement). That central launchpad is SAP Build Work Zone.

The Scene: Two Keys Needed for Every User

Our user, Maria, works in Procurement. To do her job, she needs access to the Create Purchase Order app.

This app lives inside the S/4HANA system, but we want her to launch it from Work Zone. This requires two distinct keys working together.

Key 1: The UI Key (Federated BTP Role Collection)

Work Zone uses content federation. It imports the S/4HANA UI content (business roles, spaces, pages and tiles) into Work Zone, so nothing has to be rebuilt manually in the cloud.

For every federated business role, a BTP role collection is generated automatically, named after the content provider ID and the backend role, e.g. ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER.

What this key does: When Maria logs in to Work Zone, her identity (via SAP Cloud Identity Services / Microsoft Entra ID) is mapped to this role collection. This lets her see and click the Purchase Order tile on her homepage. This key only gets her into the lobby of the building.

Key 2: The Data Key (Backend PFCG Role)

Maria clicks the tile. The app is now running and needs to read and write live data in S/4HANA.

Principal propagation through the SAP Cloud Connector securely passes Maria's identity down to S/4HANA. S/4HANA maps it to her local user (SU01) and checks: does Maria have the PFCG role SAP_BR_PURCHASER (and its authorizations) in this system?

What this key does: If the role is assigned, she is authorized to work with the specific business data. This key opens the locked office door and gives access to the actual files.

Configuration Walkthrough

Below are the steps I followed to set this up end to end. Names such as s4h and S4H_RT are examples; use your own naming conventions.

Step 1: Expose the business roles in S/4HANA

  1. Make sure the business roles you want to federate (e.g. SAP_BR_PURCHASER) have their launchpad spaces and pages assigned.
  2. Open transaction /UI2/CDM3_EXP_SCOPE, select the roles and choose Expose.
  3. Repeat the exposure whenever the roles, spaces or pages change, so Work Zone can pick up the updates.

Step 2: Connect S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector

  1. In the Cloud Connector, add a Cloud to On-Premise mapping to your S/4HANA system (protocol HTTPS, virtual host and port).
  2. Set Principal Type to X.509 Certificate so that principal propagation is possible.
  3. Expose the required resource paths, typically /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/, /sap/opu/odata/, /sap/opu/odata4/, /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/ and /sap/public/bc/.
  4. Under Configuration > On Premise, create the system certificate and the CA certificate for principal propagation, and synchronize trust with your subaccount.

Step 3: Trust the Cloud Connector in S/4HANA

  1. Import the Cloud Connector CA/system certificate into the SSL server PSE in STRUST.
  2. Set the ICM profile parameters icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_issuer and icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_subject to the issuer and subject of the Cloud Connector system certificate, then restart the ICM.
  3. In CERTRULE, create a rule that maps the short-lived user certificate (e.g. the CN or e-mail) to the SU01 user. This is where Maria's cloud identity becomes her backend user.

Step 4: Create the destinations in the BTP subaccount

  • Design-time destination (e.g. S4H_DT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>/sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/entities, Proxy Type OnPremise, authentication with a technical user (or principal propagation), plus the property sap-client. Work Zone uses it to fetch the exposed content.
  • Runtime destination (e.g. S4H_RT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>, Proxy Type OnPremise, Authentication PrincipalPropagation, plus sap-client and HTML5.DynamicDestination = true. Apps use it when Maria opens them. Point the runtime destination for OData to the same destination unless your landscape separates them.

Step 5: Add S/4HANA as a content provider in Work Zone

  1. In the Site Manager, open the Channel Manager and choose New > Content Provider.
  2. Enter a title and an ID (e.g. s4h; this becomes the prefix of the generated role collections), and select the design-time and runtime destinations.
  3. Choose whether to include all exposed roles or only selected ones, and save. Wait until the status shows the content was fetched successfully.
  4. In the Content Manager > Content Explorer, open the provider, select the roles and choose Add to My Content.
  5. Assign the roles to your site in the Site Settings.

Step 6: Assign both keys to the user

  • Key 1 (BTP): In the BTP cockpit under Security > Role Collections, assign ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER to Maria, or better, map it to an IdP group so assignments are managed centrally in your identity provider.
  • Key 2 (S/4HANA): Make sure Maria's SU01 user exists with the same identity used in the CERTRULE mapping, and assign SAP_BR_PURCHASER in PFCG/SU01.

Quick troubleshooting checklist

  • Tile is not visible: the BTP role collection is missing, the role is not assigned to the site, or the content was not re-fetched after a change in S/4HANA.
  • Tile is visible but the app fails with 401/403: check the Cloud Connector principal propagation setup, the CERTRULE mapping and the PFCG role assignment in S/4HANA.
  • Content provider fails to fetch: test the design-time destination and check that /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/ is exposed in the Cloud Connector.

Conclusion

You cannot replace one key with the other. Federated BTP role collections exist for operational efficiency: they bring the launchpad layout from S/4HANA into Work Zone automatically, so you do not replicate catalogs and spaces by hand. PFCG roles exist for security: they enforce the data-level authorizations in the system of record. When a user reports "I can see the tile but the app doesn't work" (or the other way around), ask which of the two keys is missing, and you will usually find the answer quickly.

In upcoming posts, I will cover other Work Zone scenarios, including apps deployed on BTP, to complete the end-to-end picture.

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: Adding XSUAA Security to a CAP Service on the BTP Trial
entry.content:
A CAP service on Cloud Foundry with "auth": "none", locked down with XSUAA, an approuter, and two role collections.

This started as part of my prep for the SAP C_CPE exam, where I got the wrong end of the stick with "auth": "none". I've since passed, and wanted to revisit the security part for my own development / sanity / stupidity.

Setup

Logistics service: Shipments and Packages, HANA Cloud HDI container, deployed to the trial dev space (us10). CAP 9.6. Anyone could call it.

Goal: two roles. Viewer reads, Admin does everything.

Logging on

cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com --sso
cf target -o <trial-org> -s dev

Adding XSUAA

cds add xsuaa

Three changes: an empty xs-security.json, an xsuaa resource in mta.yaml, and a production profile in package.json:

"[production]": { "auth": "xsuaa" }

Local cds watch still runs without a login. On CF, NODE_ENV=production switches on token checks.

Roles in the CDS

srv/logistics-service.cds:

service LogisticsService @(path: '/logistics') {

    // Viewer can read, Admin can do anything
    @restrict: [
        { grant: 'READ', to: 'Viewer' },
        { grant: '*',    to: 'Admin'  }
    ]
    entity Shipments as projection on my.Shipments;

    // read-only entity, either role can see it
    @readonly
    @requires: ['Viewer', 'Admin']
    entity Packages as projection on my.Packages;
}

Then generate the role templates from the model:

cds compile srv --to xsuaa > xs-security.json

Two scopes ($XSAPPNAME.Viewer, $XSAPPNAME.Admin), two role templates. $XSAPPNAME is replaced at deploy time.

Approuter

cds add approuter

Creates app/router/. Without it a browser just gets 401 - the service only accepts requests that already carry a token. The approuter does the login and passes the token on (forwardAuthToken: true).

Deploying with cf push

Without mta.yaml, the app name and redirect URIs have to go in xs-security.json itself. Added at the top:

"xsappname": "c-cpe-dev",
"tenant-mode": "dedicated",
"oauth2-configuration": {
  "redirect-uris": ["https://*.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
},

XSUAA instance:

cf create-service xsuaa application c-cpe-auth -c xs-security.json

Service - build, bind, push over the existing app (keeps its route and HDI binding):

npx cds build --production
cf bind-service <srv-app> c-cpe-auth
cf push <srv-app> -p gen/srv -b nodejs_buildpack -m 256M

Straight call with no token:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://<srv-route>/logistics/Shipments
401

Approuter. app/router/default-env.json points at localhost:4004 for local runs, so it's kept out of the upload:

cd app/router
printf 'default-env.json\nnode_modules\n' > .cfignore
cf push cpe-router -b nodejs_buildpack -m 256M --random-route --no-start
cf bind-service cpe-router c-cpe-auth
# destination the approuter forwards to - the CAP service route
cf set-env cpe-router destinations '[{"name":"srv-api","url":"https://<srv-route>","forwardAuthToken":true}]'
cf start cpe-router

Roles and role collections in the cockpit

Subaccount > Security > Roles, search c-cpe. Admin and Viewer under application c-cpe-dev, description "generated" from CAP.

 

Security > Role Collections > Create. Two collections: CPE Viewer, CPE Admin.

 

Open the collection, Edit. In Roles, value help, filter Application Identifier to c-cpe-dev!t<id> (BTP adds the !t suffix). Tick the role, Add.

 

In Users, enter the email in ID and E-Mail, Default identity provider, Save.

 

CPE Viewer got the Viewer role and one user, CPE Admin the Admin role and another.

Working

entry.title: Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model on SAP BTP: Who Owns What?
entry.content:
When you move workloads to SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), one of the first governance questions you need to answer is deceptively simple: who is responsible for what?

It's a question that often goes unanswered until something goes wrong - a security incident, a compliance gap, an outage that exposes unclear ownership. The SAP BTP Admin Guide addresses this head-on with a clearly defined Shared Responsibility Model and understanding it is foundational to operating on the platform safely and effectively.

It's Not a Two-Party Model - It's Three

Most teams think of shared responsibility as a binary: SAP handles the platform; we handle our apps. But SAP BTP involves three distinct parties:

 

What SAP Is Responsible For

As the service provider, SAP is responsible for the following areas:

  • Global Accounts and Entitlements Provisioning

SAP creates your global account and assigns the necessary entitlements so you can start using SAP BTP. During this provisioning process, SAP grants initial global account administrator rights to your designated administrator.

  • Runtimes and Services Management

SAP manages and operates the core BTP services and runtimes - including Cloud Foundry, SAP Integration Suite, and SAP Build - and keeps them updated and secure. Depending on the runtime you use, you share responsibility differently: Kyma gives you full cluster access except the SAP-managed Kyma-system namespace, while the ABAP environment lets you manage select aspects via the Landscape Portal.

 

What You Are Responsible For

As an SAP BTP customer, you’re responsible for the following areas:

  • Change Management and Operations

You establish and run effective change management processes for your applications and integrations. If you use open-source software, you must keep it updated and include vulnerability scanning in your development process.

  • Customer Data and Content

You are responsible for your data and content, which includes ensuring data privacy.

  • Application Development and Integration

You develop and operate your applications on SAP BTP. This includes creating, deploying, and integrating them with other systems.

  • Account and Environment Management

You manage your account structure, which includes organizing directories, subaccounts, and service instances. You define an account strategy based on your organization's requirements, create and configure subaccounts for your development projects, and allocate resources and services as needed.

  • Authorization and Identity Management

You manage users and assign authorizations according to your organizational and project needs. To meet these needs, use the authorization and identity management tools that SAP provides.

 

The Shared Zones: Where Collaboration Is Essential

You and SAP share responsibility for the following key areas:

  • Observability

SAP handles platform-level monitoring for all BTP services - covering health checks, troubleshooting, housekeeping, and incident management. As a customer, you're expected to leverage BTP's built-in monitoring tools, add your own checks where needed, and manage housekeeping for your own components. If an issue falls under SAP's responsibility, raise an incident through the standard SAP support process.

  • Security and Compliance

SAP treats security and compliance as a core priority on BTP. They adhere to strict industry standards across cybersecurity, operations, and privacy, and manage risks through comprehensive programs that cover cloud environments, physical facilities, events, and employees - ensuring your data is protected and regulatory requirements are met.

  • High Availability and Disaster Recovery

SAP guarantees high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR) for all SAP-managed BTP services through strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs), regular backups, and built-in disaster recovery mechanisms. However, customers also carry responsibility -particularly when deploying custom applications and extensions. This includes running a minimum of three instances where applicable and configuring SAP HANA Cloud with replicas to ensure resilience and for the overall HA/DR setup to work as intended.

 

Infrastructure Provider's Responsibilities

The infrastructure level is managed by either SAP or a hyperscaler, with SAP overseeing the relationship with hyperscalers. Even when using hyperscaler regions, SAP is responsible for managing this relationship. As a customer using SAP BTP, you don't have to interact directly with the hyperscalers.

The infrastructure providers operate the physical data centers that host SAP BTP regions. Their responsibilities include:

  • Set up and maintain the data centers, including servers, networking, and power supply.
  • Ensure physical and digital security to prevent unauthorized access.
  • Meet industry-grade standards for reliability and compliance.
  • Manage infrastructure operations, including software updates and patches.

 

Why This Model Matters in Practice

For Enterprise Architects and BTP administrators, the shared responsibility model is not just a governance document - it is an operational checklist. It drives decisions about:

  • Team structure: Who in your organization owns account governance? Who owns application security? Are those roles clearly defined and staffed?
  • Security controls: Are you applying SAP's security recommendations at the application and identity layer, or assuming the platform handles it all?
  • Compliance posture: Regulators will ask what you did to protect data - "SAP is responsible for the platform" will not cover application-layer gaps
  • Incident readiness: When something goes wrong, do you have the audit logs, monitoring, and runbooks to respond within your scope - or will you be scrambling to understand what you own?

 

📔Further Reading:

  • Shared Responsibility Model Between You and SAP — SAP BTP Admin Guide
  • SAP Trust Center
  • Resilience, High Availability, and Disaster Recovery

 

SAP's Customer Quality Check (CQC) services - the Security Optimization Service (SOS) and Transport Execution Analysis (TEA) - give customers a structured, expert-led way to fulfil their side of the shared responsibility model on SAP BTP. SOS surfaces misconfigured security settings across your BTP landscape with prioritized, actionable recommendations, while TEA identifies risks in how changes move through your environment. Together, they turn the abstract concept of shared responsibility into something measurable and manageable - available to customers on SAP Enterprise Support or Mission Critical Support.

  • SAP Community blog: Introducing Self-Service Booking in SAP for Me
  • Watch this short overview video
  • Explore the Services & Support FAQs
  • SAP Support Portal Continuous Quality Check & Improvement Services

 

🔗Stay connected 

Want to stay up to date on our services? Join our SAP Cloud ALM & Cross-Solution Topics community! 

🔔Stay tuned for my upcoming blogs based on Operating Model, SAP BTP Security Recommendations.

entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.
